title: Define release artifact matrix + naming + checksum layout
description:
# Goal
Define the **canonical release artifact contract** for `brenner`:
- which targets we build
- how files are named
- where/how checksums are published

This contract is the bridge between:
- the release workflow (producer)
- `install.sh` / `install.ps1` (consumer)
- `brenner doctor` (verification)

# Target choices (decision points)
- Linux x64: `bun-linux-x64-baseline` vs `modern` (baseline is safer).
- Whether we ship a separate musl binary (`bun-linux-x64-musl`) or keep glibc-only for v0.
- macOS: arm64 + x64.
- Windows: x64.

# Naming scheme (proposal)
Make it deterministic and grep-able:
- `brenner-${os}-${arch}` (optionally `-baseline` / `-musl` suffixes)
- Checksums: either `brenner-${...}.sha256` per artifact **or** a single `SHA256SUMS` file.

# Acceptance criteria
- A written mapping exists (table is fine) that lists:
  - supported (os, arch) tuples
  - bun compile `--target` values
  - resulting artifact filenames
  - checksum filename conventions
- The mapping is referenced by `brenner_bot-5so.11.2.1` (install.sh) and the toolchain manifest.
close_reason: Defined release artifact matrix: targets, naming scheme, checksum format, URL templates. Updated toolchain manifest with linux-arm64.

title: Implement GitHub Actions release workflow (binaries + checksums)
description:
# Goal
Add a **tag-driven release workflow** that builds `brenner` binaries and publishes them as GitHub release assets.

# Why
This enables the installer fast-path:
- `install.sh` can download a pinned `vX.Y.Z` artifact
- the download is verifiable via checksum

# Requirements
- Trigger on tags like `v*`.
- Build the target matrix from `brenner_bot-5so.5.5.3`.
- Compile using `bun build --compile --target=... --outfile ... ./brenner.ts`.
- Generate SHA256 checksums for every artifact and upload alongside.

# Optional (nice-to-have)
- Attach `install.sh` / `install.ps1` (and their `.sha256`) to the release so users can fetch installers by tag.
- `workflow_dispatch` dry-run mode that builds artifacts without publishing.

# Acceptance criteria
- A tag build produces:
  - binaries
  - checksum files
  - a GitHub release containing those assets
- The release artifact names match the installer mapping.
close_reason: release.yml builds tagged binaries+checksums; workflow_dispatch now uploads dist artifact and does not publish unless running on a tag

title: Release: publish installers + checksums as release assets
description:
# Goal
Make releases self-contained for bootstrapping:
- tag releases publish **binaries + checksums** (already in scope)
- and also publish **installers + installer checksums**

This enables a safer pinned install flow:
- `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<org>/<repo>/<tag>/install.sh | bash -s -- ...`
- optionally verify `install.sh` against `install.sh.sha256` from the release

---

# Reference patterns
- `cass` dist workflow copies `install.sh` and `install.ps1` into `dist/` and attaches them to the GitHub release.
- `cm` release workflow uploads `install.sh.sha256` alongside binaries.

---

# Design notes
Publishing installer checksums doesn’t make `curl|bash` perfect, but it:
- makes audits easier
- allows CI/offline consumers to verify the exact installer script
- nudges users toward pinned-tag installs rather than `main`

---

# Acceptance criteria
- Release workflow uploads:
  - `install.sh`
  - `install.ps1` (if present)
  - `install.sh.sha256` (and optionally `install.ps1.sha256`)
- README documents a pinned-tag install option.
close_reason: release.yml uploads install.sh/install.ps1 + sha256 alongside binaries; README already documents pinned-tag install

# Goal
Integrate the cass memory system so sessions can:
- retrieve relevant procedural rules + past insights
- augment kickoffs with retrieved context
- (later) feed durable artifacts back into memory

---

# Why this matters
Brenner-style work compounds. Memory prevents re-deriving the same primitives and enables cumulative research.

---

# Constraints / integration stance
- **No vendor AI APIs required.** Brenner Bot should rely on `cm context`’s deterministic scoring + cass search.
- **Fail-soft**: if `cm` is missing/unconfigured, sessions still run.
- **Local-first**: memory is best-effort in local lab / cockpit workflows; do not assume it exists in hosted public web deployments.

---

# Design principle
Treat `cm` output as “memory says …” (provenance-labeled), never as transcript-grounded truth.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Findings (2025-12-30):

1) Where Agent Mail stores the archive
- The Agent Mail server maintains a separate git-backed mailbox repo (not inside this workspace).
- On this machine it lives at:
  `~/.mcp_agent_mail_git_mailbox_repo/projects/data-projects-brenner-bot/`
  and contains:
  - `messages/YYYY/MM/*.md` (canonical message bodies + JSON header)
  - `messages/threads/*.md` (thread rollups)
  - `agents/<Name>/profile.json`
  - `file_reservations/…`

2) Can cass index Agent Mail archives directly?
- Out-of-the-box: effectively **no**.
- `cass diag --json` shows cass indexes known “session” sources only (Codex/Claude/Gemini/etc):
  - codex: `~/.codex/sessions`
  - claude: `~/.claude/projects`
  - gemini: `~/.gemini/tmp`
- After `cass index --full --json`, `cass stats --json` shows only agents: `claude_code`, `codex`, `gemini` (no Agent Mail connector), and searches return hits from session logs, not from `~/.mcp_agent_mail_git_mailbox_repo/...`.
- Passing the mailbox path to `cass index --watch-once <path>` does not add a new source type; it only reindexes supported session sources.

3) Recommended approach (practical)
- Treat cass as the index for *agent execution logs* (Codex/Claude/Gemini sessions).
- Treat Agent Mail as the durable coordination archive and use either:
  - Agent Mail search (`search_messages` tool), or
  - local grep on the mailbox repo, e.g.:
    `rg -n "<THREAD_ID>" ~/.mcp_agent_mail_git_mailbox_repo/projects/data-projects-brenner-bot/messages`

4) If we truly want cass-search over Agent Mail threads
- We likely need an **export step** (Agent Mail → a cass-ingestible format). Options:
  - Export each thread to a synthetic Codex-style `.jsonl` (or a new cass connector) and index it.
  - Or store exported thread text in a dedicated “sessions” directory that cass is explicitly taught to ingest.
- Suggest handling as follow-up in brenner_bot-5so.6.5.2.

title: Content policy: transcript rights + public vs private mode
description:
# Goal
Before putting the full transcript corpus on `brennerbot.org`, decide what is:
- public
- gated (lab mode)
- never served

---

# Why this matters
- transcripts may have redistribution constraints
- the public site should be legally and ethically clean

---

# Current status (working decision)
- Full transcripts: CONDITIONAL NO-GO for public hosting without explicit permission.
- Public mode: serve only an explicit allowlist (distillations + method docs + short excerpts if legally safe).
- Lab mode: gated access for restricted docs + all orchestration side-effects.

---

# Required outputs
1. A clear policy document embedded in the repo (could be a page in the web app and/or a short markdown in root) describing:
   - what is public
   - what is gated
   - what is never served
2. Enforcement mechanisms in the web app:
   - allowlist
   - locked UX for restricted docs
   - no direct access to restricted raw files
3. Attribution/terms page.
4. Outreach to Web of Stories for permission to host transcripts.

---

# Acceptance
- A contributor can tell immediately whether a given document may be served publicly.
- Public deployment cannot accidentally expose restricted docs.

Brenner optimized for **evidence per week** and cheap, decisive moves.

- reduce context-switching overhead
- make parallel hypotheses cheap
- make it easy to compare representations across models

title: Bug: Edge proxy should gate Cloudflare Access header trust
description:
# Goal
Define a safe execution environment for running agent-generated experiment code against target repositories.

# The Gap
The other agent identified "experiment execution loop" but didn't address SAFETY. Agent-generated code is untrusted:
- Could have bugs that corrupt data
- Could consume unbounded resources
- Could make unintended network calls
- Could modify files outside the experiment scope

# Why This Matters
Without sandboxing:
- Agents can't safely generate and run experiments
- Human must manually review ALL generated code
- Risk of data loss or system compromise
- Can't automate the evidence loop

With sandboxing:
- Agents can propose experiments that get executed safely
- Failed/malicious experiments are contained
- Results are captured cleanly
- Enables automation of the evidence loop

# Proposed Implementation

## Isolation Model
```yaml
# experiment-sandbox.yaml
isolation:
  type: container  # or VM for higher isolation
  image: python:3.12-slim  # or project-specific
  
resource_limits:
  cpu: 2 cores
  memory: 4GB
  time: 300s  # 5 minute max
  disk: 1GB
  
network:
  enabled: false  # no outbound by default
  allowed_hosts: []  # whitelist if needed
  
filesystem:
  read_only:
    - /target_repo  # experiment can READ target
  read_write:
    - /results      # experiment writes here
  blocked:
    - /etc
    - /root
    - /.git        # prevent git operations
```

## Execution Protocol
```typescript
interface ExperimentExecution {
  experiment_id: string;
  session_id: string;
  
  // What to run
  command: string;           // e.g., "python run_test.py"
  working_dir: string;       // e.g., "/target_repo"
  env: Record<string, string>;
  
  // Safety constraints
  sandbox_config: SandboxConfig;
  
  // Outputs
  results: {
    stdout: string;
    stderr: string;
    exit_code: number;
    duration_ms: number;
    resource_usage: ResourceMetrics;
    artifacts: string[];     // files written to /results
  };
}
```

## CLI Integration
```bash
# Run experiment in sandbox
./brenner.ts experiment run \
  --session RS-20251230-bio-rrp \
  --command "python tests/test_rrp.py" \
  --timeout 300 \
  --no-network

# Check experiment status
./brenner.ts experiment status --id exp-001
```

# Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Sandbox config schema defined
- [ ] Container-based isolation implemented
- [ ] Resource limits enforced
- [ ] Network isolation by default
- [ ] Results captured to structured format
- [ ] CLI commands for experiment execution
- [ ] Failed experiments don't affect host system

# Relationship to Other Work
- Depends on: Target repository binding
- Enables: Results → DELTA encoding
- Complementary to: Experiment execution loop (from other agent)

title: Feature: Hypothesis Lifecycle States
description:
# Feature: Hypothesis Lifecycle States

## Purpose
Implement the state machine that governs hypothesis lifecycle transitions. The Brenner method treats hypotheses as temporary entities that should be "killed" — this feature formalizes that process.

## Background
From Sydney Brenner's methodology:
- §229: "When they go ugly, kill them. Get rid of them." — Hypotheses MUST be killable
- §103: "Both could be wrong" — Third alternatives are first-class citizens
- §147: "Exclusion is always a tremendously good thing" — The goal is to reduce the hypothesis space

A hypothesis is not a thing to be proven, but a thing to be tested and, ideally, eliminated.

## State Machine Design

```
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │  proposed   │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │ activate
                           ▼
                    ┌─────────────┐
            ┌───────│   active    │───────┐
            │       └──────┬──────┘       │
            │ refine       │ test         │ park
            ▼              │              ▼
     ┌─────────────┐       │       ┌─────────────┐
     │  refined    │       │       │   dormant   │
     └─────────────┘       │       └─────────────┘
            │              │              │
            │              ▼              │ reactivate
            │     ┌────────────────┐      │
            │     │ test executed  │      │
            │     └───────┬────────┘      │
            │             │               │
            │    ┌────────┴────────┐      │
            │    ▼                 ▼      │
     ┌─────────────┐       ┌─────────────┐
     │   killed    │       │  validated  │
     └─────────────┘       └─────────────┘
```

## State Definitions

1. **proposed** — Initial state. Hypothesis has been stated but not yet accepted for investigation.
2. **active** — Under active investigation. Tests are being designed/executed against it.
3. **refined** — Replaced by a more precise version. Links to child hypothesis.
4. **killed** — Invalidated by a test result. Terminal state (no resurrection!).
5. **validated** — Survived a discriminative test designed to kill it. Rare and provisional.
6. **dormant** — Parked for later. Not killed, but not actively investigated.

## Transition Rules

| From | To | Trigger | Requirements |
|------|-----|---------|--------------|
| proposed | active | activate | None |
| proposed | dormant | park | Optional reason |
| active | refined | refine | Must link to child hypothesis |
| active | killed | kill | Must link to test result |
| active | validated | validate | Must link to test result |
| active | dormant | park | Optional reason |
| dormant | active | reactivate | None |
| refined | (none) | — | Terminal state |
| killed | (none) | — | Terminal state |
| validated | refined | refine | New evidence prompts refinement |
| validated | killed | kill | New test invalidates |

## Implementation

### State Transition Function
```typescript
interface StateTransition {
  hypothesisId: string;
  fromState: HypothesisState;
  toState: HypothesisState;
  trigger: 'activate' | 'refine' | 'kill' | 'validate' | 'park' | 'reactivate';
  triggeredBy?: string;  // Test ID or user
  reason?: string;
  timestamp: string;
}

function transitionHypothesis(
  hypothesis: Hypothesis,
  toState: HypothesisState,
  trigger: StateTransition['trigger'],
  metadata?: Partial<StateTransition>
): Result<Hypothesis, TransitionError>
```

### Transition History
- Every state change is recorded in a transition log
- Enables: "show me the history of hypothesis H1"
- Enables: "what killed H1? when?"

### CLI Commands
- `brenner hypothesis activate <id>` — Move from proposed to active
- `brenner hypothesis kill <id> --test=<test-id> --reason="..."` — Kill with evidence
- `brenner hypothesis refine <id> --child=<new-id>` — Replace with refined version
- `brenner hypothesis history <id>` — Show transition history

## Success Criteria
- [ ] State transitions are validated (no invalid transitions)
- [ ] All transitions are logged with timestamp and trigger
- [ ] CLI commands for all valid transitions
- [ ] Transition history is queryable
- [ ] Terminal states (killed, refined) cannot be un-done

## Depends On
- brenner_bot-XXXX: Hypothesis Registry Schema (for base types)

## Non-Goals
- Automatic state transitions based on test results (that's Test→Hypothesis Binding)
- UI for state visualization (later feature)
close_reason: Implemented hypothesis lifecycle state machine with: state transitions (proposed→active→confirmed/refuted/superseded/deferred), transition validation, requirements enforcement (testResultId for refute/confirm, childHypothesisId for supersede), TransitionHistoryStore for audit logging, and 72 passing unit tests. Follows Brenner method principles from §229, §103, §147.

All 5 rich markdown prompt files (~32 KB total) exist right next to `index.ts` in `apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/prompts/`. However, `fetchPromptContent()` only reads `specs/role_prompts_v0.1.md`, which only contains markers for `adversarial_critic` and `test_designer`. Consequently, `loadPrompt('statistician')`, `loadPrompt('brenner_channeler')`, and `loadPrompt('synthesis')` always return literal placeholder strings `[Prompt at: prompts/...]`.

## Implementation Plan
1. Sync/copy the 5 markdown files from `apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/prompts/*.md` into `apps/web/public/_corpus/prompts/*.md` so they are served statically in browser/Vercel environments alongside the rest of `/_corpus/`.
2. Update `fetchPromptContent()` in `apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/index.ts` so that:
   - First, it attempts to load the dedicated role markdown file (`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/prompts/<file>.md` or `public/_corpus/prompts/<file>.md` on Node/server, and `/_corpus/prompts/<file>.md` in the browser).
   - Second, it falls back to extracting markers from `specs/role_prompts_v0.1.md` if needed.
   - Only falls back to `[Prompt at: ...]` if neither source is available.

## Verification & Test Gate
- Update `apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/agents.test.ts` to assert that `loadPrompt(role)` for every role in `TRIBUNAL_ORDER` (`devils_advocate`, `experiment_designer`, `statistician`, `brenner_channeler`, `synthesis`) returns real markdown prompt content (>500 chars) and never `[Prompt at: ...]`.
close_reason: Wired all 5 Tribunal Agent prompts (devils_advocate, experiment_designer, statistician, brenner_channeler, synthesis) to load real markdown prompts from prompts/*.md and specs/role_prompts_v0.1.md across Node/Bun/Vitest and browser public/_corpus/prompts/, verified by unit tests.

title: Epic: TanStack Library Integration
description:
# Epic: TanStack Library Integration

## Vision
Transform the Brenner Bot web app's data layer, rendering performance, and state management by adopting the TanStack ecosystem. This is a strategic investment that will:
- **Eliminate redundant work**: Stop re-parsing the 473KB transcript on every page load
- **Improve performance**: Virtualize long document rendering (236 transcript sections to ~10 visible)
- **Enhance UX**: Persist reading positions, filter states, and user preferences
- **Reduce code complexity**: Replace ~500 lines of manual caching/state logic with battle-tested libraries

## Why TanStack?
TanStack libraries are the gold standard for React data management:
1. **Designed to work together**: Query, Virtual, Table, Form, Store share patterns
2. **Framework-agnostic core**: Not locked to React, future-proof
3. **Excellent TypeScript support**: Better DX than alternatives
4. **Active maintenance**: Widely adopted (40M+ downloads/week)
5. **Small bundle impact**: ~40KB gzipped total for all libraries we need

## Strategic Context
The Brenner Bot web app is reading-first. Users spend most time:
1. Reading the 236-section transcript
2. Comparing 3 model distillations
3. Browsing the quote bank
4. (Less frequently) Creating research sessions

## Success Metrics
1. Transcript page TTI < 1s (currently ~3s on slow networks)
2. Bundle size: < 50KB gzipped additional
3. Code reduction: Remove ~500 lines of manual cache/state logic
4. UX: Reading position persists across sessions

title: CLI: ignore invalid implicit config file
description:
## Problem
`brenner.ts` loads a default config file path (`~/.config/brenner/config.json` or `%APPDATA%\brenner\config.json`) even when the user did not explicitly opt in. If that file exists but is malformed JSON (or has wrong shape), the CLI hard-fails.

## Why this is bad
From a first-principles UX/reliability standpoint:
- The *default* behavior should be resilient: a stray/half-written config file should not brick the CLI.
- Explicit config (`--config` or `BRENNER_CONFIG_PATH`) should remain strict (fail fast) to avoid silently ignoring operator intent.

## Root cause
`loadBrennerConfig()` parses config unconditionally when the default path exists; parse errors throw.

## Fix
- If config path is **implicit** (default) and parsing fails, **fail-soft**: ignore the config and continue with env + defaults.
- If config path is **explicit** (`--config` or `BRENNER_CONFIG_PATH`), keep **fail-fast** behavior.
- Optionally emit a one-line warning to stderr when ignoring an implicit config (must not spam normal output).

## Acceptance
- `--config <path>` with invalid JSON => exit 1 with a clear parse error.
- Default path exists but invalid JSON => CLI still works (exit codes/outputs unchanged for normal commands).
- Unit tests cover the explicit/implicit behavior boundary.
close_reason: Fail-soft on invalid implicit config; fail-fast on explicit config; add bun tests

title: Task: Add interactive mode to "brenner test execute"
description:
# Goal
Add an interactive prompt flow for `brenner test execute TEST_ID` so operators can record executions without manually specifying every flag.

This is a UX layer on top of the existing non-interactive (flag-driven) implementation.

---

# Background / Why
`brenner test execute` is the bridge between an executed discriminative test and hypothesis state updates (confirm/refute). In practice, the operator often has the observation in hand but doesn’t want to translate it into multiple CLI flags.

We already have:
- test records + execution recording (stored under `.research/tests/`)
- transition suggestions (kill/validate)
- optional auto-apply (`--apply`)

Missing: a first-class, low-friction operator UX for entering those fields interactively.

---

# Proposed UX (interactive mode)
When invoked as:

```bash
brenner test execute T-...
```

Prompt for:
1) Observed result/observation (free text)
2) Potency check: pass/fail (required)
3) Confidence: high/medium/low/speculative (default: medium)
4) Optional notes
5) (Optional / v0) “Apply suggested transitions?” (yes/no)
   - If yes: apply all or review one-by-one

Non-goal: running experiments. This command only records and binds results.

---

# CLI surface decisions
- Keep the existing flag-driven path working exactly as-is.
- Add `--interactive` to force prompts even if some flags are present.
- Add `--no-interactive` (or equivalent) to fail fast if required flags are missing (useful for scripts/CI).
- Ensure `--json` works in both modes (final output emitted as one JSON object).

---

# Implementation constraints
- Bun-only; no vendor AI APIs.
- Avoid adding heavy prompt dependencies if possible; prefer `node:readline`/stdin-based prompting.
- Ensure prompts do not trigger in non-TTY contexts unless explicitly requested (avoid hanging pipelines).

---

# Testing
Add CLI tests that drive stdin for interactive prompts. Approach:
- Extend the `runCli(...)` helper in `brenner.test.ts` to optionally write to stdin.
- Create a minimal temp project with a ready test + active hypotheses.
- Run `brenner test execute T-... --json` with scripted stdin input and assert:
  - execution recorded
  - suggestions returned
  - (if apply chosen) hypothesis states updated

---

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `brenner test execute TEST_ID` prompts for required execution fields when run interactively.
- [ ] Non-interactive usage via flags continues to work unchanged.
- [ ] Non-TTY runs do not hang (either require flags or require `--interactive`).
- [ ] Tests cover at least one interactive happy path (stdin-driven).
close_reason: Added interactive mode tests for 'brenner test execute'. Tests verify stdin prompts work for result, potency check, confidence, notes, and apply suggestions. Tests pass (140/140).

title: Content: Define Brenner Operators glossary entries (14 terms)
description:
# Brenner Operators Glossary Entries

## Goal
Write glossary entries for all 14 Brenner operators. Each needs:
- term: Display name with symbol
- short: One-liner for tooltip
- long: Plain-English explanation
- analogy: "Think of it like..." for non-scientists
- why: Relevance to scientific discovery
- related: 2-4 related operator/concept keys

## Terms to Define

### 1. level-split (⊘)
Separate program from interpreter; message from machine.
Example: DNA (program) vs ribosome (interpreter); "chastity vs impotence" distinction.

### 2. recode (𝓛)
Change representation/coordinates to make problem tractable.
Example: 3D protein folding → 1D genetic sequence problem.

### 3. invariant-extract (≡)
Find what survives coarse operations; use physics to kill cartoons.
Example: What survives across species = fundamental; what varies = implementation.

### 4. exclusion-test (✂)
Design experiments that eliminate whole model families at once.
Example: "If overlapping code, adjacent amino acid pairs would be forbidden."

### 5. object-transpose (⟂)
Change organism/system until the decisive experiment becomes cheap.
Example: Switch from mammals to C. elegans for developmental biology.

### 6. amplify (↑)
Use selection, dominance, regime switches to get "across the room" differences.
Example: Choose systems where signal is 50-70% of total, not 0.1%.

### 7. cross-domain (⊕)
Import tools/encodings from other fields to break monopolies.
Example: Apply information theory to molecular biology.

### 8. paradox-hunt (◊)
Use contradictions as beacons; start where the model can't be true.
Example: "How can DNA be 1mm in a 1μm cell?" → folding mechanism.

### 9. exception-quarantine (ΔE)
Isolate anomalies explicitly without hiding or destroying coherent theory.
Example: Note exceptions in ledger; don't sweep under carpet.

### 10. dephase (∿)
Work out of phase with scientific fashion; stay in opening game.
Example: Avoid crowded fields; find problems others haven't noticed.

### 11. theory-kill (†)
Drop hypotheses aggressively when nature says no.
Example: "Don't fall in love with your theory; be willing to kill it."

### 12. materialize (⌂)
Compile stories into decision procedures: "What would I see if this were true?"
Example: Transform verbal theory into concrete experimental prediction.

### 13. diy (🔧)
Build what you need; don't wait for infrastructure.
Example: Brenner's crude apparatus that worked vs elegant apparatus never built.

### 14. scale-check (⊞)
Calculate; stay imprisoned in physics; filter impossible cartoons.
Example: "Can this actually work at the relevant scale and timescale?"

## Writing Guidelines
- Avoid jargon in definitions (recursive problem!)
- Use concrete examples from Brenner's work
- Make analogies accessible to educated non-scientists
- Reference transcript §n anchors where applicable

## Deliverable
Add entries to `apps/web/src/lib/jargon.ts` under "operators" category.
close_reason: Enhanced all 19 Brenner operators with transcript §n anchors and added 3 derived operators (Quickie, HAL, Potency-Check)

description:
# Task: Create Hypothesis CLI Commands

## Objective
Implement CLI commands for managing hypotheses: list, show, create, link, search.

## Implementation Details

### File Location
Add to `brenner.ts` CLI or create `apps/web/scripts/hypothesis-cli.ts`

### Commands

#### `brenner hypothesis list`
```bash
brenner hypothesis list [--state=<state>] [--session=<id>] [--format=table|json]

# Examples:
brenner hypothesis list
brenner hypothesis list --state=active
brenner hypothesis list --session=RS-20251230
```

Output:
```
ID                  | State  | Statement (truncated)
--------------------|--------|----------------------------------
H-RS20251230-001    | active | Cell fate is epigenetically...
H-RS20251230-002    | killed | Methylation is the only...
H-RS20251231-001    | active | Third alternative: chromatin...
```

#### `brenner hypothesis show <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis show H-RS20251230-001

# Output:
Hypothesis: H-RS20251230-001
Statement: Cell fate is epigenetically determined by methylation patterns
  established during early development.

State: active
Origin: proposed
Session: RS-20251230
Proposed by: BlueLake (codex-cli)
Created: 2025-12-30T10:00:00Z
Updated: 2025-12-30T10:00:00Z

Tags: epigenetics, cell-fate, methylation
Notes: Initial hypothesis from paradox discussion.

Linked Tests:
  - T-RS20251230-001: Lineage tracing with Cre-lox (designed)
  - T-RS20251230-002: Single-cell ATAC-seq (completed)

Parent: (none)
Children: H-RS20251231-001 (refinement)
```

#### `brenner hypothesis create`
```bash
brenner hypothesis create \
  --session=RS-20251230 \
  --statement="Cell fate is epigenetically determined" \
  --origin=proposed \
  [--parent=<id>] \
  [--proposed-by=<agent>] \
  [--tags=tag1,tag2]
```

#### `brenner hypothesis link <child-id> <parent-id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis link H-RS20251231-001 H-RS20251230-001
# Links H-RS20251231-001 as a refinement of H-RS20251230-001
```

#### `brenner hypothesis search <query>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis search "epigenetic"

# Output:
Found 3 hypotheses matching "epigenetic":
  H-RS20251230-001: Cell fate is epigenetically determined... [active]
  H-RS20251231-001: Third alternative: chromatin accessibility... [active]
  H-RS20251230-002: Methylation is the only epigenetic... [killed]
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 5 commands implemented and documented
- [ ] `--help` works for each command
- [ ] JSON output format for scripting
- [ ] Error handling for invalid IDs, missing files
- [ ] Tab completion hints where possible

## Dependencies
- Task: Define Hypothesis Zod Schema
- Task: Implement Hypothesis Storage Layer

## Effort Estimate
~300 lines of code, ~3 hours

description:
# Task: Implement Hypothesis Storage Layer

## Objective
Create the file-based storage layer for hypotheses with JSON persistence and cross-session indexing.

## Implementation Details

### File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/hypothesis-storage.ts`

### Storage Structure
```
.research/
├── hypotheses/
│   ├── RS-20251230-hypotheses.json  # Per-session file
│   ├── RS-20251231-hypotheses.json
│   └── ...
└── hypothesis-index.json  # Cross-session lookup
```

### Per-Session File Format
```json
{
  "sessionId": "RS-20251230",
  "hypotheses": [
    {
      "id": "H-RS20251230-001",
      "statement": "Cell fate is epigenetically determined",
      "origin": "proposed",
      "state": "active",
      "createdAt": "2025-12-30T10:00:00Z",
      "updatedAt": "2025-12-30T10:00:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "lastModified": "2025-12-30T10:00:00Z"
}
```

### Index File Format
```json
{
  "hypotheses": {
    "H-RS20251230-001": {
      "sessionId": "RS-20251230",
      "statement": "Cell fate is epigenetically determined",
      "state": "active"
    }
  },
  "lastRebuilt": "2025-12-30T12:00:00Z"
}
```

### Core Functions
```typescript
// Read/write operations
export async function loadSessionHypotheses(sessionId: string): Promise<Hypothesis[]>
export async function saveSessionHypotheses(sessionId: string, hypotheses: Hypothesis[]): Promise<void>

// Index operations
export async function rebuildHypothesisIndex(): Promise<void>
export async function getHypothesisById(id: string): Promise<Hypothesis | null>
export async function searchHypotheses(query: string): Promise<Hypothesis[]>

// CRUD helpers
export async function addHypothesis(hypothesis: Hypothesis): Promise<void>
export async function updateHypothesis(id: string, updates: Partial<Hypothesis>): Promise<void>
```

## Design Decisions
1. **File-per-session**: Keeps diffs clean, allows partial sync
2. **Separate index**: Fast lookups without loading all files
3. **JSON format**: Human-readable, git-friendly
4. **Async API**: Future-proofs for potential DB backend

title: Tutorial Content: Domain Examples (Biology, CS, Social Science)
description:
# Purpose

Create worked examples showing the Brenner method applied to different domains. Users learn best by seeing the method in action on problems similar to their own.

---

# Why Domain Examples Matter

The Brenner method was developed in molecular biology, but its power is domain-transferability. To convince users from other fields, we need to show:

1. **It works outside biology** - The operators and artifact structure apply to CS, physics, social science
2. **Different domains highlight different operators** - Biology emphasizes object-transposition; CS emphasizes level-split
3. **Users can pattern-match to their domain** - "Oh, this is like my problem!"

---

# Required Examples

## Example 1: Biology (Brenner's Home Turf)
**Topic**: "How do cells determine their fate during development?"

**Why this one**: 
- Directly from Brenner's work
- Rich with his vocabulary (morphogens, gradients, positional information)
- Users can compare their output to the "master's" thinking

**Artifact highlights**:
- Hypothesis slate: gradient model vs timing model vs stochastic model + third alternative
- Tests: object-transposition to C. elegans or zebrafish
- Assumptions: diffusion timescales, scale constraints
- §n anchors: §58, §78, §161

## Example 2: Computer Science
**Topic**: "Why do large language models hallucinate?"

**Why this one**:
- Directly relevant to BrennerBot's likely user base
- Shows level-split in action (training vs inference vs architecture)
- Testable with experiments on actual models

**Artifact highlights**:
- Hypothesis slate: capacity/compression, RLHF misalignment, distributional shift + third alternative (maybe hallucination is a feature not bug)
- Tests: controlled experiments on model behavior
- Assumptions: what counts as "hallucination"?
- Cross-domain import from cognitive science

## Example 3: Social Science
**Topic**: "Why do some online communities become toxic?"

**Why this one**:
- Shows method works for "soft" sciences too
- Different experimental constraints (can't do RCTs on communities)
- Emphasizes exclusion tests with observational data

**Artifact highlights**:
- Hypothesis slate: moderation failure, selection effects, platform incentives + third alternative
- Tests: natural experiments, cross-platform comparisons
- Assumptions: definition of "toxic", measurement validity
- Scale check: individual vs group vs platform level

---

# Deliverables

For each example:
1. **Research question** (1 paragraph)
2. **Excerpt** (5-10 §n citations or domain-specific evidence)
3. **Complete artifact** (all 7 sections)
4. **Operator annotations** (which operators were used where)
5. **Commentary** (why this artifact is "good")

## File Structure
\`\`\`
lib/tutorial-data/examples/
├── biology-cell-fate.ts
├── cs-llm-hallucination.ts
└── social-community-toxicity.ts
\`\`\`

---

# Quality Criteria

- Each example passes the linter
- Third alternatives are genuinely different (not strawmen)
- Tests are actually feasible
- Assumptions include scale checks
- §n citations are relevant (not just vocabulary matching)
- Commentary explains the "why" behind each section

---

# Usage in Tutorial

- Quick Start Step 7: "Here's what a good artifact looks like" (link to biology example)
- Agent-Assisted Step 8: Compare agent output to examples
- Method page: Examples as case studies
- Standalone /examples page for browsing
close_reason: Added tutorial domain examples (biology/CS/social) with lintable artifacts + /tutorial/examples pages

title: TanStack Virtual: Virtualize TranscriptViewer Sections
description:
# Goal Virtualize the TranscriptViewer to only render visible sections, reducing DOM nodes from 236 to ~10. ## Why Priority 0? The transcript is the MOST viewed page. It contains 236 sections. Currently all render at once causing: - Slow initial paint (3+ seconds on slow devices) - Janky scrolling - High memory usage - Poor Core Web Vitals This is the single highest-impact performance optimization. ## Current Implementation ```typescript // TranscriptViewer.tsx {data.sections.map((section, index) => (
{ sectionRefs.current[index] = el; }}>
))} ``` This renders ALL 236 sections into the DOM. ## Target Implementation ```typescript import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual'; function TranscriptViewer({ data }) { const parentRef = useRef(null); const virtualizer = useVirtualizer({ count: data.sections.length, getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current, estimateSize: () => 200, // Estimated section height overscan: 3, // Render 3 extra above/below viewport }); return (
{virtualizer.getVirtualItems().map((virtualRow) => { const section = data.sections[virtualRow.index]; return (
); })}
); } ``` ## Key Challenges ### 1. Variable Height Sections Sections have different heights (some are 2 lines, some are 20). Solution: Use `measureElement` for dynamic measurement. ### 2. Scroll Position Restoration When navigating back, should restore scroll position. Solution: Integrate with TanStack Store (later task). ### 3. Active Section Tracking Currently uses IntersectionObserver to track which section is visible. Solution: Virtual provides `scrollToIndex` and we can derive active from virtualizer state. ### 4. TOC Navigation Clicking TOC item should scroll to that section. Solution: `virtualizer.scrollToIndex(index, { align: 'start' })` ### 5. URL Hash Links Direct links like `/corpus/transcript#section-42` should work. Solution: On mount, parse hash and scroll to index. ## Considerations ### Scroll Container Transcript uses `window` scroll currently. Virtual works best with a dedicated scroll container. Trade-off: Slightly different feel, but much better performance. ### SSR Compatibility Virtual is client-only. Need to handle hydration: - Option A: Render first N sections on server, virtualize on client - Option B: Render placeholder, full virtualize on client ### Reading Progress The ReadingProgress component calculates scroll percentage. With virtualization, calculate from `virtualizer.scrollOffset` instead. ## Performance Metrics Before: - 236 DOM nodes for sections - ~3s initial render on slow devices After: - ~13 DOM nodes for sections (10 visible + 3 overscan) - <500ms initial render - 95% reduction in DOM size ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] TranscriptViewer uses Virtual - [ ] Only visible sections render (verify in DevTools) - [ ] Scrolling is smooth at 60fps - [ ] TOC navigation works - [ ] URL hash links work - [ ] Reading progress still works - [ ] Active section highlighting works ## Files to Modify - apps/web/src/components/transcript/TranscriptViewer.tsx - apps/web/src/components/transcript/ReadingProgress.tsx (adapt to virtual) - apps/web/src/components/transcript/TableOfContents.tsx (scrollToIndex)
close_reason: Virtualization implemented with useVirtualizer, build and tests pass

title: Content: Define Core Brenner Concepts (6 terms)
description:
# Core Brenner Concepts Glossary Entries

## Goal
Write glossary entries for the foundational vocabulary used throughout BrennerBot.

## Terms to Define

### 1. brenner-move
A recurring reasoning pattern in Sydney Brenner's methodology.
Examples: Hunt paradoxes, invert the problem, choose the right experimental object.

### 2. decision-experiment
An observation designed to eliminate whole families of explanations at once.
Contrast with: Incremental experiments that only nudge probabilities.

### 3. digital-handle
A readout that is effectively yes/no, robust to noise, high leverage.
Example: Binary phenotype (alive/dead) vs continuous measurement (slightly different).

### 4. representation-change
Restating the problem in a domain where constraints are clearer.
Example: Shifting from chemistry to information theory; 3D to 1D.

### 5. assumption-ledger
Explicit list of load-bearing assumptions + tests that would break them.
Contrast with: Implicit assumptions hidden in theoretical framework.

### 6. third-alternative
The "both models are wrong" option; guard against false dichotomies.
Example: Not "A or B" but "what if the question itself is wrong?"

## Writing Guidelines
- These are the vocabulary users will encounter constantly
- Definitions should be memorable and usable
- Include why Brenner used each concept

## Deliverable
Add entries to `apps/web/src/lib/jargon.ts` under "brenner" category.

## Problem & Context
1. `apps/web/src/app/sessions/[threadId]/operators/page.tsx` stores operator inputs only in ephemeral React state and never persists to `sessionStorage`, nor does it offer the guided multi-step operator wizards (`LevelSplitSession`, `ExclusionTestSession`, `ObjectTransposeSession`, `ScaleCheckSession`).

## Implementation Plan
1. In `operators/page.tsx`: Hydrate hypothesis context and completed operators from `sessionStorage.load(threadId)`, persist completed operators back to `sessionStorage`, and provide a toggle between 'Quick Worksheet' and 'Guided Interactive Wizard' (`LevelSplitSession`, `ExclusionTestSession`, `ObjectTransposeSession`, `ScaleCheckSession`).
2. In `agents/page.tsx`: Load hypothesis & operator results from `sessionStorage`, allow viewing/copying each agent's real system prompt + ready-to-run `ntm send` command via `loadPrompt()` and `buildAgentPrompt()`, and wire the 'Generate Full Synthesis' button to compute and display a live `SynthesisResult` via `synthesizeResponses()`.
3. In `brief/page.tsx`: Dynamically build brief sections from `sessionStorage.load(threadId)`, `loadTestQueue(threadId)`, and `loadAssumptionLedger(threadId)` when present (falling back to `BASE_BRIEF_SECTIONS` when no stored session exists), and wire `Preview` (markdown preview dialog), `Share` (copy shareable summary/URL), and `Print` (`window.print()`).

## Verification & Test Gate
- Add unit tests for `operators/page.tsx`, `agents/page.tsx`, and `brief/page.tsx` verifying persistence, NTM prompt inspection, synthesis generation, and brief preview/print actions.

title: Content: Define Bayesian/Statistical terms (12 terms)
description:
# Bayesian/Statistical Glossary Entries

## Goal
Write glossary entries for Bayesian and statistical concepts that underpin Brenner's implicit methodology.

## Terms to Define

1. **prior**: Initial probability before seeing evidence
2. **posterior**: Updated probability after incorporating evidence
3. **likelihood**: Probability of evidence given a hypothesis
4. **likelihood-ratio**: Ratio comparing how well two hypotheses explain evidence
5. **bayesian-reasoning**: Updating beliefs systematically as evidence accumulates
6. **expected-information-gain**: How much uncertainty an experiment should reduce
7. **kl-divergence**: Measure of difference between probability distributions
8. **probability-mass**: Amount of probability assigned to outcomes
9. **model-misspecification**: When all considered models are wrong
10. **prior-distribution**: Full distribution of initial beliefs
11. **posterior-distribution**: Full distribution after updating
12. **marginal-likelihood**: Probability of evidence averaged over hypotheses

## Writing Guidelines
- Brenner didn't use Bayesian formalism, but his reasoning maps to it
- Define for non-statisticians with intuitive explanations
- Connect each term to how Brenner-style reasoning embodies it

## Deliverable
Add entries to `apps/web/src/lib/jargon.ts` under "bayesian" category.

title: Bug: compile should surface missing delta code fences (inline deltas)
description:
## Problem
Pilot sessions showed agents sometimes post inline JSON that *looks* like a delta but is not wrapped in a fenced code block (```delta ... ```). The delta parser then extracts zero blocks and compilation drops the intended update (or produces an incomplete artifact), creating confusing operator UX.

## Goal
Make compilation fail loudly (or at least warn prominently) when a DELTA[role] message contains **no parseable delta blocks**, and provide actionable remediation.

## Proposed fix
- During compile (web `/api/sessions/actions` + CLI `brenner session compile`):
  - For each message with subject prefix `DELTA[` (per thread subject conventions), attempt delta extraction.
  - If extractedBlocks == 0, treat as a hard compile error (preferred) OR an error-level violation surfaced prominently.
  - Include message author + timestamp + a short snippet + a copy/paste template showing the required fenced format.
- Add targeted unit tests covering: inline-json-without-fence, empty delta message, and correct fenced delta.

## Acceptance
- A DELTA[role] message with zero extracted delta blocks triggers a clear, deterministic failure (not silent drop).
- Error output identifies the specific message(s) and how to fix.
- Existing compile tests updated; web + CLI builds/tests pass.
close_reason: Fail-fast on DELTA messages with 0 parseable delta blocks in web compile + CLI compile; added targeted tests.

title: TanStack Store: Migrate useLocalStorage Hook to Store
description:
# Goal
Migrate the existing useLocalStorage hook to use TanStack Store for consistency.

## Background
We have a custom useLocalStorage hook:
```typescript
// apps/web/src/hooks/useLocalStorage.ts
export function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initialValue: T) {
  const [storedValue, setStoredValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    try {
      const item = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
      return item ? JSON.parse(item) : initialValue;
    } catch {
      return initialValue;
    }
  });
  // ...
}
```

After implementing TanStack Store for reading positions and compare state, we should:
1. Evaluate if useLocalStorage is still needed
2. Either delete it or have it use Store internally
3. Ensure consistency across all persisted state

## Decision Matrix

| Use Case | Current | After TanStack Store |
|----------|---------|---------------------|
| Reading positions | N/A (none) | readingStore |
| Compare state | N/A (none) | compareStore |
| User preferences | useLocalStorage | preferencesStore |
| Form drafts | N/A | Could use Store |

## Options

### Option A: Delete useLocalStorage
If all use cases are covered by specific stores, delete the generic hook.
Simpler, but less flexible.

### Option B: Keep as Utility
Keep useLocalStorage for one-off values that don't need a store.
E.g., "dismissed welcome banner" flag.

### Option C: Make Store-backed
Reimplement useLocalStorage to use a generic Store internally.
Best of both worlds.

## Recommendation
Option B: Keep useLocalStorage for simple boolean flags, use Store for complex state.

## Migration Steps
1. Audit all uses of useLocalStorage
2. Move complex state to dedicated stores
3. Keep hook for simple flags
4. Document when to use which

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All complex persisted state uses TanStack Store
- [ ] useLocalStorage only used for simple values
- [ ] No duplicate persistence logic
- [ ] Clear documentation on when to use what

## Files to Evaluate
- apps/web/src/hooks/useLocalStorage.ts
- Any component using useLocalStorage
close_reason: Migration complete: Removed duplicate useReadingPosition from useLocalStorage.ts (TanStack Store version in useReadingPosition.ts is the canonical one). Added documentation explaining when to use useLocalStorage (simple flags) vs TanStack Store (complex state). The readingStore pattern is already established and working.

title: Spec: External Evidence Import Protocol
description:
# Goal
Define the protocol for importing external evidence (papers, datasets, prior experiment results, benchmark data) into Brenner Loop sessions as citable, structured inputs.

## The Gap This Fills

Other agents covered:
- **Topic corpus ingestion** - PRIMARY sources for a research domain (like Brenner transcripts for the method itself)
- **Results → DELTA encoding** - How OUR experiment outputs become deltas
- **Target repository binding** - How sessions connect to codebases

**What nobody covered:** How do EXTERNAL evidence sources enter the system? Specifically:

1. A paper was published last week that refutes hypothesis H2 - how does that enter the session?
2. A benchmark dataset exists that could serve as a potency check - how do we reference it?
3. A colleague ran an experiment outside this system and has results - how do we import them?
4. A prior Brenner Loop session (different project) produced relevant findings - how do we cite it?

This is different from "topic corpus" because:
- Topic corpus = domain knowledge you READ to inform hypotheses
- External evidence = RESULTS that validate/refute hypotheses

## Why This Matters for Real Science

Real research constantly references external evidence:
- "Smith et al. (2024) showed X, which supports H1"
- "The ImageNet benchmark demonstrates Y"
- "Our collaborators experiment found Z"

Without a formal import mechanism, agents can only:
1. Reference their training data (not auditable, may be stale)
2. Hallucinate citations (dangerous)
3. Ignore external evidence entirely (limiting)

## Proposed Solution

### 1. Evidence Types

```typescript
type EvidenceType = 
  | "paper"           // Published research paper
  | "preprint"        // Unpublished manuscript
  | "dataset"         // Structured data (benchmark, corpus, etc.)
  | "experiment"      // Results from an experiment (internal or external)
  | "observation"     // Empirical observation without formal experiment
  | "prior_session"   // Results from another Brenner Loop session
  | "expert_opinion"  // Human expert statement
  | "code_artifact";  // Existing code/implementation as evidence
```

### 2. Evidence Record Structure

```typescript
interface ExternalEvidence {
  id: string;           // E.g., "EV-001" or DOI
  type: EvidenceType;
  
  // Citation info
  title: string;
  authors?: string[];
  date: string;
  source: string;       // URL, DOI, file path, or session ID
  
  // Access
  access_method: "url" | "file" | "agent_mail" | "api";
  access_path: string;
  
  // Content summary
  abstract?: string;    // Human-readable summary
  key_findings: string[]; // Bulleted findings relevant to session
  
  // Relationship to session
  imported_at: string;
  imported_by: string;  // Agent or operator who added it
  relevance: string;    // Why this evidence matters to this session
  
  // Targeting
  supports?: string[];  // Item IDs this evidence supports (e.g., ["H1", "T3"])
  refutes?: string[];   // Item IDs this evidence refutes
  informs?: string[];   // Item IDs this evidence is relevant to
  
  // Verification
  verified: boolean;    // Has someone confirmed this evidence is real/accurate?
  verification_notes?: string;
}
```

### 3. Import Protocol

#### Via CLI:
```bash
# Import a paper by DOI
brenner evidence import --type paper --doi "10.1234/example" --relevance "Supports H1 mechanism"

# Import experiment results from file
brenner evidence import --type experiment --file results.json --supports H1,H4 --refutes H2

# Import from prior session
brenner evidence import --type prior_session --session "RS-20251228-initial" --item H3
```

#### Via Agent Mail:
```markdown
Subject: EVIDENCE: External paper supports H1

```evidence
{
  "type": "paper",
  "title": "Synaptic vesicle depletion dynamics in attention mechanisms",
  "doi": "10.1234/example",
  "key_findings": [
    "RRP depletion follows exponential decay",
    "Recovery time constant ~500ms matches our T1 predictions"
  ],
  "supports": ["H1"],
  "relevance": "Provides empirical basis for vesicle depletion timescales"
}
```​
```

### 4. Evidence in Artifacts

Artifacts gain a new section:

```markdown
## External Evidence

| ID | Type | Source | Supports | Refutes | Key Finding |
|----|------|--------|----------|---------|-------------|
| EV-001 | paper | doi:10.1234/ex | H1 | - | RRP decay matches predictions |
| EV-002 | dataset | benchmarks/synthetic_rep.json | T5 | - | Provides test stimuli |
| EV-003 | prior_session | RS-20251228-initial | - | H2 | H2 was killed after T3 |
```

### 5. Evidence Validation

Agents and operators can challenge evidence:
- "Is this paper peer-reviewed?"
- "Is this dataset properly documented?"
- "Can we verify these experiment results?"

Unverified evidence is marked and treated with lower confidence.

### 6. Integration with Deltas

Deltas can reference evidence:

```json
{
  "operation": "KILL",
  "section": "hypothesis_slate",
  "target_id": "H2",
  "payload": {
    "kill_reason": "Contradicted by external evidence EV-001 and EV-003"
  },
  "evidence_refs": ["EV-001", "EV-003"]
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `ExternalEvidence` type defined in session/artifact types
- [ ] Evidence section added to artifact schema
- [ ] CLI `brenner evidence import` command with --type, --source, --supports, --refutes
- [ ] Agent Mail EVIDENCE: message type with structured payload parsing
- [ ] Evidence references allowed in delta blocks
- [ ] Artifact lint validates evidence references (warns on missing EV-xxx)
- [ ] Web UI shows evidence in session detail
- [ ] Evidence verification workflow (mark verified/unverified)

## Dependencies

- Artifact schema (exists)
- Delta parser (needs extension for evidence_refs)
- Independent of experiment execution (evidence can be imported without running experiments)

## Non-Goals

- Not building a full citation manager (use Zotero/etc. for that)
- Not automatically fetching paper content (just referencing)
- Not implementing evidence strength scoring (thats evaluation rubric territory)

## Example Use Case

Research question: Does vesicle depletion in bio_inspired_nanochat behave like biological synapses?

1. Operator imports paper on synaptic vesicle dynamics (EV-001)
2. Operator imports benchmark dataset for repetition detection (EV-002)
3. Agent references EV-001 in proposing H1 ("our implementation matches biological timescales")
4. Another agent challenges: "EV-001 was in vitro, not in silico - relevance unclear"
5. Test T4 designed to compare our implementation against EV-002 dataset
6. Results of T4 imported as EV-003, which refutes H2
7. Final artifact shows complete evidence chain for conclusions

title: Build Hypothesis Intake Form (Socratic Refinement)
description:
# Build Hypothesis Intake Form (Socratic Refinement)

## Purpose
Create the initial hypothesis entry experience that guides users through proper formulation.

## The Problem
Most hypotheses arrive malformed:
- "Social media causes depression"
- "AI will take all jobs"
- "Meditation is good for you"

These are vague, non-falsifiable, and confound multiple mechanisms.

## The Socratic Approach
Guide users through refinement:

### Step 1: Initial Statement
> "Enter your hypothesis"
> [                                    ]

### Step 2: Mechanism
> "What specific mechanism are you proposing?"
> □ Content exposure → mood change
> □ Social comparison → self-esteem
> □ Displacement of other activities
> □ Algorithm-driven engagement loops
> □ Other: [________________]

### Step 3: Predictions If True
> "If your hypothesis is CORRECT, what would we observe?"
> [Add observations that MUST be true if you're right]

### Step 4: Predictions If False
> "If your hypothesis is WRONG, what would we observe?"
> [Add observations that would indicate you're wrong]

### Step 5: Falsification Conditions (Critical)
> "What observation would PROVE YOU WRONG — not just weaken
>  your hypothesis, but definitively rule it out?"
> 
> This is crucial. If you can't answer, your hypothesis
> isn't testable yet.
> 
> [Add at least one falsification condition]

### Step 6: Initial Confidence
> "How confident are you? (0-100)"
> [Slider or input]
> 
> Note: High confidence should mean you've already
> thought about how you could be wrong.

title: FEATURE: Competing Hypotheses Arena - Head-to-Head Comparison
description:
# Competing Hypotheses Arena - Head-to-Head Comparison

## The Gap This Fills
The current design tracks a single hypothesis through evolution. But Brenner's approach fundamentally involves **comparing competing hypotheses against each other**:

> "The question is not whether your hypothesis is consistent with the data, but whether it's MORE consistent than the alternatives." — paraphrased from §89

Without competing hypotheses, users default to confirmation bias: "Does my hypothesis fit?" instead of "Does my hypothesis fit BETTER than alternatives?"

## Feature Design

### Hypothesis Arena
```typescript
interface HypothesisArena {
  id: string;
  question: string;  // The research question being addressed
  
  // Competing hypotheses
  competitors: HypothesisCard[];
  
  // Shared evidence
  sharedEvidence: EvidenceEntry[];  // Tests that apply to all
  
  // Comparison matrix
  testResults: {
    testId: string;
    hypothesisId: string;
    result: 'supports' | 'challenges' | 'neutral';
  }[];
  
  // Rankings
  currentRanking: { hypothesisId: string; score: number }[];
  eliminatedHypotheses: { hypothesisId: string; eliminatedBy: string }[];
}
```

### Key Features

#### 1. Multiple Hypothesis Entry
When Object Transpose generates alternatives, they become REAL competitors:
- H₀: Original hypothesis
- H₁: Reverse causation version  
- H₂: Third variable version
- H₃: User-added alternative

Each gets tracked as a first-class hypothesis with its own predictions.

#### 2. Shared Test Application
When recording evidence, user selects which hypotheses the test applies to:
- "This test discriminates between H₀ and H₁"
- "This test challenges both H₀ and H₂"
- "This test supports H₁ but is neutral to others"

#### 3. Elimination Tracking
When a hypothesis fails a strong test:
- Mark as "Eliminated"
- Record which test eliminated it
- Show in the "Graveyard" (see related feature)
- Celebrate the narrowing of possibility space

#### 4. Comparison Matrix View
```
            Test 1    Test 2    Test 3    Status
H₀          ✓ +5%     ✗ -20%    ?         Active (52%)
H₁          ✓ +8%     ✓ +5%     ?         Active (71%)
H₂          ✗ -15%    —         —         Eliminated
```

#### 5. Brenner Scoring
Hypotheses that make BOLD predictions should get bonus credit:
- Hypothesis predicted something specific → higher multiplier
- Hypothesis hedged → lower multiplier
- "The bolder the prediction, the more informative the test"

### Integration Points
- Object Transpose → Creates initial competitors
- Evidence Ledger → Records per-hypothesis results
- Agent Tribunal → Evaluates all competitors
- Research Brief → Shows elimination history

## Why This is Critical
Without competing hypotheses, the system enables confirmation bias. With them, it forces discriminative thinking — the core Brenner insight.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Can have 2+ hypotheses competing on same question
- [ ] Tests can be applied across hypotheses
- [ ] Elimination is tracked and visible
- [ ] Comparison matrix shows relative standings
- [ ] Eliminated hypotheses are preserved for learning
close_reason: Implemented HypothesisArena with competing hypotheses, test tracking, elimination, and comparison matrix

title: FEATURE: Hypothesis Graveyard - Learning from Falsification
description:
# Hypothesis Graveyard - Learning from Falsification

## The Gap This Fills
When a hypothesis is falsified, the current system just updates confidence to near-zero. But Brenner would say:

> "Being proven wrong is not a failure — it's the most informative outcome. You've eliminated a possibility and narrowed the search space."

The system should CELEBRATE falsification and extract maximum learning value.

## Feature Design

### Graveyard Data Model
```typescript
interface FalsifiedHypothesis {
  id: string;
  hypothesis: HypothesisCard;
  
  // Death certificate
  falsifiedAt: Date;
  killingBlow: EvidenceEntry;  // The test that did it
  deathType: DeathType;
  
  // Learning extraction
  lessonsLearned: string[];
  whatWeNowKnow: string[];
  whatRemainsOpen: string[];
  
  // Legacy
  successorHypotheses: string[];  // What came next
  contributedTo: string[];        // Other hypotheses informed by this death
  
  // Epitaph
  epitaph: string;  // User's summary of what was learned
  brennerQuote?: string;  // Relevant Brenner wisdom
}

type DeathType = 
  | 'direct_falsification'    // Impossible observation occurred
  | 'mechanism_failure'       // Proposed pathway doesn't work
  | 'effect_size_collapse'    // Effect is too small to matter
  | 'superseded'              // Better hypothesis emerged
  | 'unmeasurable'            // Can't be tested with current methods
  | 'scope_reduction';        // Valid only in narrow conditions
```

### Key Features

#### 1. Dignified Death Ceremony
When a hypothesis is falsified:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🪦 HYPOTHESIS FALSIFIED                                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│  "Algorithm-driven content selection causes clinical        │
│   depression in teenagers"                                  │
│                                                             │
│  Killed by: Natural Experiment - Algorithm Change 2021     │
│  Observation: Depression rates rose BEFORE algorithm change│
│                                                             │
│  Brenner says: "This is not a failure. This is progress.  │
│  You now know something you didn't before."                │
│                                                             │
│  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════   │
│                                                             │
│  What did we learn?                                        │
│  [                                                    ]    │
│                                                             │
│  What remains open?                                        │
│  [                                                    ]    │
│                                                             │
│  What should we try next?                                  │
│  ○ Reverse causation hypothesis                            │
│  ○ Third variable hypothesis                               │
│  ○ Refined mechanism hypothesis                            │
│  ○ Something else: [                              ]        │
│                                                             │
│  [Generate Successor Hypothesis] [Archive to Graveyard]    │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 2. Graveyard Gallery
View all falsified hypotheses:
- Organized by topic/domain
- Searchable
- Shows what was learned from each
- Links to successor hypotheses

#### 3. Learning Extraction
Prompt users to document:
- What assumption was wrong?
- What does this tell us about the phenomenon?
- What's still possible?
- What new questions arise?

#### 4. Failure Pattern Analysis
Across sessions:
- "50% of psychology hypotheses fail due to reverse causation"
- "Most failures happen at the mechanism test"
- "Users who do Level Split first have fewer failures"

#### 5. Graveyard Achievements
Gamification that celebrates learning:
- 🪦 "First Blood" - First hypothesis falsified
- ⚰️ "Hypothesis Hunter" - 5 hypotheses properly falsified
- 🎓 "Learned Humility" - Revised hypothesis after falsification
- 🔬 "Scientific Method" - Falsification led to better hypothesis

### Why This is Critical
Most tools hide failure. This tool should celebrate it because:
- Falsification is the most informative outcome
- Learning from failure prevents repeat mistakes
- Graveyard creates institutional memory
- Celebrating failure reduces ego investment

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Falsified hypotheses get dignified ceremony
- [ ] Learning extraction is prompted
- [ ] Graveyard is searchable and browsable
- [ ] Successor hypotheses are linked
- [ ] Failure patterns are analyzed
close_reason: Implemented graveyard data model with FalsifiedHypothesis types, FalsificationCeremony wizard component, and HypothesisGraveyard gallery component. Includes Brenner quotes, validation, statistics, and failure pattern analysis.

title: FEATURE: Assumption Ladder - Dependency Mapping & Cascade Analysis
description:
# Assumption Ladder - Dependency Mapping & Cascade Analysis

## The Gap This Fills
The HypothesisCard has an "assumptions" field, but it's just a list. Missing:
- Which assumptions are load-bearing?
- If assumption A fails, does the whole hypothesis fail?
- Can assumptions be tested independently?
- What's the cascade of failure?

## Feature Design

### Assumption Structure
```typescript
interface Assumption {
  id: string;
  hypothesisId: string;
  
  // Content
  statement: string;
  rationale: string;  // Why do we assume this?
  
  // Classification
  type: AssumptionType;
  criticality: 'foundational' | 'important' | 'minor';
  
  // Dependencies
  dependsOn: string[];  // Other assumption IDs
  failureCascade: string[];  // What fails if this fails
  
  // Testability
  testable: boolean;
  testStrategy?: string;
  linkedTests?: string[];  // Test IDs
  
  // Status
  status: 'assumed' | 'tested' | 'validated' | 'invalidated';
  confidence: number;
  
  // Evidence
  supportingEvidence?: string[];
  challengingEvidence?: string[];
}

type AssumptionType = 
  | 'causal_structure'   // X causes Y (not reverse)
  | 'measurement'        // We can measure X accurately
  | 'population'         // Effect applies to this population
  | 'mechanism'          // This is how X causes Y
  | 'temporal'           // Timing assumptions
  | 'scope'              // Effect applies in these conditions
  | 'background'         // Implicit assumptions
  | 'methodological';    // Assumptions about our approach
```

### Assumption Ladder View
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ASSUMPTION LADDER                                          │
│  Your hypothesis rests on these assumptions                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│  ⚠️ FOUNDATIONAL (if wrong, hypothesis fails)               │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ A1: Causation runs X → Y (not Y → X)                  │ │
│  │ Status: Assumed (untested)                            │ │
│  │ If wrong: Entire hypothesis invalid                   │ │
│  │ [Test This] [Mark Validated]                          │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ A2: Depression can be validly measured by PHQ-9      │ │
│  │ Status: Validated (established in literature)         │ │
│  │ If wrong: Outcome measurement invalid                 │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                             │
│  ⚡ IMPORTANT (if wrong, hypothesis weakened)               │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ A3: Effect applies to all teens (not just subgroup)  │ │
│  │ Status: Assumed (untested)                            │ │
│  │ If wrong: Hypothesis scope reduced                    │ │
│  │ [Test This]                                           │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                             │
│  📝 MINOR (if wrong, minor adjustment needed)               │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ A4: Effect is linear (not threshold-based)           │ │
│  │ Status: Assumed                                       │ │
│  │ [Test This]                                           │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                             │
│  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════   │
│  DEPENDENCY MAP                                             │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│                                                             │
│       [A1: Causation] ─────┬──────> [Hypothesis]           │
│             │              │                               │
│             v              │                               │
│       [A2: Measurement] ───┘                               │
│             │                                               │
│             v                                               │
│       [A3: Population]                                     │
│                                                             │
│  If A1 fails: Entire branch invalidated                    │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key Features

#### 1. Automatic Assumption Extraction
During hypothesis intake, prompt for assumptions:
- "What are you assuming about causation?"
- "What measurement assumptions are you making?"
- "What population does this apply to?"

#### 2. Dependency Mapping
Users specify:
- "A1 is foundational — if wrong, everything fails"
- "A3 depends on A2"
- Visual graph of dependencies

#### 3. Cascade Analysis
If an assumption is invalidated:
- Show what else fails
- Update hypothesis status
- Suggest salvage options

#### 4. Assumption Testing Integration
Each assumption can:
- Generate tests in Test Queue
- Link to Evidence Ledger entries
- Update status based on evidence

#### 5. Assumption-Based Confidence
Confidence should factor in assumption status:
- All foundational assumptions validated → confidence boost
- Key assumption untested → confidence capped
- Foundational assumption invalidated → hypothesis fails

### Integration Points
- Hypothesis Intake → Captures assumptions
- Exclusion Test → Can target assumptions
- Evidence Ledger → Updates assumption status
- Research Brief → Shows assumption ladder

## Why This is Critical
Most hypotheses fail at their assumptions, not their core claim. By making assumptions explicit and testable:
- Users identify weak points early
- Cascade failures are understood before they happen
- Testing can be prioritized by assumption criticality
- The real burden of proof becomes clear

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Assumptions captured during intake
- [ ] Criticality classification works
- [ ] Dependency map visualized
- [ ] Cascade analysis shows failure paths
- [ ] Assumptions can be independently tested
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met: (1) Assumptions captured during intake via Step 6 of HypothesisIntake.tsx, (2) Criticality classification with foundational/important/minor dropdown, (3) Dependency map visualized via AssumptionDependencyMap component, (4) Cascade analysis with computeAssumptionCascadePreview showing downstream impact, (5) Independent assumption testing with test draft UI in AssumptionLadderInput. Backend fully implemented in assumption.ts, assumption-lifecycle.ts, assumption-storage.ts.

title: Spec: Cross-workspace target binding (future / v1)
description:
# Goal (future)
Define an **optional v1** mechanism to bind a session (thread + artifact) living in one Agent Mail project to a *different* target workspace (code repo / dataset workspace).

---

# v0 decision (current)
For Science Mode v0 we do **not** implement cross-workspace binding.

Instead:
- The Agent Mail `project_key` (absolute directory) *is* the research workspace.
- Start sessions in the repo/folder you’re studying.

This yields the same practical effect with less complexity.

---

# Why this could still be valuable later
Cross-workspace binding is only worth it if we need one or more of these:
- a “central session catalog” that lives in a single repo
- browsing/search across many target repos from one UI
- sessions that intentionally study multiple repos at once

If we don’t need those, keep using the v0 workspace model.

---

# Sketch (v1)
A `SessionBinding` would be purely metadata + UX sugar:
- it should not create cross-project file reservations by default
- it should not auto-run code

Example shape:
```ts
interface SessionBinding {
  thread_id: string;
  session_project_key: string; // where Agent Mail thread lives
  target_project_key: string;  // what repo/workspace is being studied
  entry_point?: string;
  default_test_command?: string;
}
```

---

# Acceptance criteria (only if we decide to do v1)
- [ ] Clear use-cases that v0 cannot satisfy
- [ ] Binding metadata persisted (kickoff + artifact metadata)
- [ ] CLI/web UX defined for setting and displaying binding
close_reason: Drafted cross-workspace binding spec in specs/cross_workspace_binding_v0.1.md

title: Task: Decide binding persistence + Agent Mail project strategy
description:
# Goal
Make an explicit design decision for how `SessionBinding` is persisted and how it interacts with Agent Mail's `project_key` model.

---

# Core question
A research session lives (conversation + artifacts) in the `brenner_bot` repo, but experiments run in a target repo.

Agent Mail projects are keyed by `human_key` (absolute directory).
We need to decide:
1) Where do the *messages* live? (almost certainly: the BrennerBot project)
2) Where do file reservations live? (BrennerBot only vs target repo too)
3) Where does the binding metadata live? (kickoff body vs compiled artifact front matter vs a dedicated binding file)

---

# Recommended stance (draft)
- Messages + thread live in **BrennerBot Agent Mail project** (single source of truth).
- Target repo binding is referenced in:
  - kickoff message body (human-visible)
  - compiled artifact YAML front matter (durable)
- File reservations:
  - optional v0: reserve in target repo by calling Agent Mail `file_reservation_paths` in the target repo's own project (requires registering the same agent name in that project)
  - do NOT split the conversation across projects

---

# Why this is worth deciding early
If we get this wrong, we break the join-key contract or make cross-repo sessions impossible to reproduce.

---

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Written decision: where binding metadata is persisted
- [ ] Written decision: whether/how we do cross-repo file reservations
- [ ] Written decision: what is considered v0 vs v1 scope
close_reason: Superseded by v0 decision: use Agent Mail project_key as the research workspace (start sessions in the repo/folder being studied); avoid cross-repo target binding in v0.

title: Task: Cross-repo file reservations (optional, advisory)
description:
# Goal
Allow the operator/orchestrator to reserve files in the target repo via Agent Mail, without moving the main thread out of BrennerBot's project.

---

# Background
File reservations prevent agent clobbering, but Agent Mail reservations are scoped to a `project_key`.
For cross-repo sessions we likely need to reserve paths in:
- BrennerBot repo (artifacts, specs)
- Target repo (code under study)

---

# Proposed approach
- Ensure the target repo is also an Agent Mail "project" (ensure_project).
- Register the same agent identity name in the target project.
- Call `file_reservation_paths(project_key=<target repo>, paths=[...])`.

---

# Risks / considerations
- This creates a second Agent Mail mailbox archive (in the target repo), but we will NOT use it for conversation.
- Needs careful UX so operators understand reservations are advisory.

---

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] CLI can reserve a path glob in the target repo project
- [ ] Failure is fail-soft (warn, do not break session) unless explicitly required
close_reason: Superseded by v0 decision: use Agent Mail project_key as the research workspace (start sessions in the repo/folder being studied); avoid cross-repo target binding in v0.

title: Content: Define Scientific Biology terms (25+ terms)
description:
# Scientific Biology Glossary Entries

## Goal
Write glossary entries for biology/genetics terms that appear throughout the corpus but which non-biologists won't know.

## Terms to Define

### Organisms
1. **c-elegans**: Caenorhabditis elegans - the nematode worm Brenner chose for developmental biology
2. **e-coli**: Escherichia coli - the workhorse bacterium of molecular biology
3. **bacteriophage**: Virus that infects bacteria (phage) - key tool for molecular genetics
4. **model-organism**: Species chosen for research because it makes experiments tractable

### Molecular Biology
5. **dna**: Deoxyribonucleic acid - the molecule that stores genetic information
6. **rna**: Ribonucleic acid - messenger molecule between DNA and proteins
7. **mrna**: Messenger RNA - the transcript of a gene
8. **genetic-code**: The mapping from nucleotide triplets to amino acids
9. **triplet-code**: The 3-nucleotide basis of genetic coding
10. **codon**: A 3-nucleotide sequence that specifies an amino acid
11. **amino-acid**: Building blocks of proteins
12. **protein**: Functional molecules encoded by genes
13. **ribosome**: Molecular machine that reads mRNA and builds proteins
14. **central-dogma**: DNA → RNA → Protein (information flows one way)

### Genetics
15. **gene**: A unit of hereditary information encoding a functional product
16. **allele**: Alternative form of a gene
17. **chromosome**: Structure containing genes (made of DNA)
18. **mutation**: Change in genetic sequence
19. **mutagenesis**: Process of inducing mutations
20. **frameshift**: Mutation that shifts the reading frame of genetic code
21. **overlapping-code**: Hypothetical code where genes share nucleotides (disproven)
22. **phenotype**: Observable characteristics of an organism
23. **genotype**: Genetic makeup of an organism
24. **complementation**: Genetic test for whether mutations are in same/different genes

### Other
25. **developmental-biology**: Study of how organisms grow and develop
26. **molecular-biology**: Study of biological molecules (DNA, RNA, proteins)

## Writing Guidelines
- Define for educated non-biologists (college-level science literacy)
- Connect to how Brenner used each concept
- Avoid circular definitions (don't use jargon to define jargon)

## Deliverable
Add entries to `apps/web/src/lib/jargon.ts` under "biology" category.

title: Task: Add scope filter (All vs Transcripts)
description:
Implement search scope filtering.

## Purpose

Users may want to:
- Search EVERYTHING (default)
- Search ONLY the original Brenner transcripts

This distinction matters because distillations are model interpretations, while transcripts are Brenner's actual words.

## UI Design

### Toggle Location
- Inside search modal, near input
- Segmented control or toggle switch
- 'All Documents' | 'Transcripts Only'

### Visual Treatment
- Clear indication of current scope
- Subtle, doesn't distract from input
- Result count updates with scope change

### Persistence
- Remember user preference in localStorage
- Restore on next session

## Implementation

### In Search Engine Wrapper
- Add scope parameter to search function
- Filter results by docType before returning

### In UI
- Add scope state to search modal
- Connect to useSearch hook
- Save/restore from localStorage

### Result Indication
- Show current scope in UI
- Perhaps filter badge: 'Searching in: Transcripts'

## User Flow

1. Open search
2. See current scope (default: All)
3. Toggle to Transcripts if desired
4. Search
5. Results filtered to scope
6. Preference remembered for next time

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Scope toggle visible in search modal
- [ ] Filtering works correctly
- [ ] Preference persisted in localStorage
- [ ] UI indicates current scope clearly
- [ ] Result counts match filter

# Goal
Do a repo-wide, first-principles review of recently landed web/CLI/installer work (from multiple agents) to catch obvious bugs, security issues, reliability problems, and protocol mismatches.

# Scope (initial)
- Installer surface: `install.sh` + toolchain manifest handling (pinning, checksum verification, shell safety).

# Approach

The agent-mail-seeder.ts imports from src/test-utils/agent-mail-test-server.ts. When test-fixtures.ts (used by all E2E tests) is loaded, even with lazy imports, the type re-export still causes module resolution at config time.
