title: Tutorial Path: Quick Start (7 Steps)
description:
# Purpose

Implement the Quick Start tutorial path — 7 steps that take a user from "What is this?" to "I have a research artifact for my own question" in approximately 30 minutes.

This is the **primary onboarding funnel**. Most users will take this path. It must be polished, failure-tolerant, and genuinely useful.

---

# Core Constraint

**No complex infrastructure required.** This path works with:
- A terminal
- Git
- Bun
- Any AI chat interface (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — even free tiers)

No Agent Mail. No ntm. No subscriptions beyond basic access.

---

# Step-by-Step Breakdown

## Step 1: What Is This? (~3 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/1/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Explain BrennerBot in 60 seconds
- Present the Two Axioms prominently
- Show a completed artifact (screenshot or inline example)
- Set expectations for the path

**Key Content**:
\`\`\`markdown
# What Is BrennerBot?

Sydney Brenner (1927-2019) was one of the most successful experimental 
biologists in history. But his **method** is more valuable than any 
single discovery.

BrennerBot operationalizes that method for AI-assisted research.

## The Two Axioms

1. **Reality has a generative grammar** — the world is produced by 
   causal machinery with discoverable rules.

2. **To understand is to reconstruct** — you haven't explained something 
   until you can build it from primitives.

## What You'll Produce

By the end of this tutorial, you'll have a **research artifact** for 
your own scientific question containing:

- 2-5 competing hypotheses (including a "third alternative")
- Discriminative tests that separate the hypotheses
- An explicit assumption ledger
- Adversarial critiques of your framing

Let's start.
\`\`\`

---

## Step 2: Prerequisites (~2 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/2/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- OS-specific instructions (tabs for Mac, Windows, Linux)
- Interactive checklist (user confirms each prereq)
- Skip affordance for experienced users

**Prerequisites**:
1. Terminal access
2. Git installed
3. Bun installed

**Code Blocks**:
\`\`\`bash
# Check git
git --version

# Check bun (or install)
bun --version || curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash

# Verify
bun --version
\`\`\`

**Troubleshooting**:
- "bun: command not found" → Add to PATH, restart terminal
- Windows: Use WSL2 (link to instructions)
- Permission errors: sudo or user install

---

## Step 3: Clone & Install (~5 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/3/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Get the repo locally
- Install dependencies
- Verify installation with doctor command

**Commands**:
\`\`\`bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/brenner_bot.git
cd brenner_bot

# Install dependencies
bun install

# Verify everything works
./brenner doctor
\`\`\`

**Expected Output**:
\`\`\`
BrennerBot Doctor Report
========================
✓ Bun runtime: 1.x.x
✓ Dependencies installed
✓ Corpus files present
✓ CLI executable
⚠ Agent Mail: not running (optional for Quick Start)
\`\`\`

**Checkpoint**: "You've cloned BrennerBot and verified your installation!"

---

## Step 4: Search the Corpus (~5 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/4/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Teach corpus search
- Show how results include §n anchors
- User searches for their own topic

**Interactive Example**:
\`\`\`bash
# Search for a topic
./brenner corpus search "pattern formation"

# Try your own domain
./brenner corpus search "YOUR_TOPIC_HERE"
\`\`\`

**Explanation**:
- Results show transcript segments with §n references
- These are stable anchors for citation
- High-quality matches ground your research in Brenner's thinking

**User Exercise**:
"Search for something related to YOUR research domain. Note 3-5 §n references that seem relevant."

---

## Step 5: Build an Excerpt (~5 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/5/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Compose relevant transcript sections into an excerpt
- Explain why excerpts matter (grounding, citation)
- Save excerpt for use in next step

**Commands**:
\`\`\`bash
# Build excerpt from specific sections
./brenner excerpt build --sections 58,78,161 > my_excerpt.md

# Or use search results to identify sections
./brenner corpus search "your topic" --format sections
./brenner excerpt build --sections THOSE_SECTIONS > my_excerpt.md
\`\`\`

**Excerpt Template**:
\`\`\`markdown
# Research Excerpt

## Relevant Brenner Segments

### §58: Reduction to one dimension
"The best thing in science is to work out of phase..."

### §78: The importance of choice
"You have to choose the right problem..."

[Your selected segments here]
\`\`\`

---

## Step 6: Your First Session (~8 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/6/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Compose a kickoff prompt using CLI
- Run in "local mode" (no Agent Mail)
- User copies output to their AI chat interface

**The Big Moment**: This is where users actually DO Brenner-style research.

**Commands**:
\`\`\`bash
# Compose a kickoff prompt (local mode)
./brenner prompt compose \\
  --excerpt-file my_excerpt.md \\
  --question "How do cells determine their position in a developing embryo?" \\
  --role unified \\
  --output-file my_prompt.md

# View the composed prompt
cat my_prompt.md
\`\`\`

**User Action**:
1. Copy the contents of my_prompt.md
2. Paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini
3. Run the conversation
4. Save the AI's response

**Pro Tip**:
"The prompt includes specific instructions for the AI to produce structured output. Don't modify these instructions — they encode the Brenner methodology."

---

## Step 7: Understand the Output (~5 min)
**File**: app/tutorial/quick-start/7/page.tsx

**Content Goals**:
- Walk through each artifact section
- Explain why each matters
- Connect back to Brenner's method

**Artifact Sections Explained**:

**Hypothesis Slate**:
- 2-5 competing explanations
- Must include "third alternative" (both leading theories could be wrong)
- Each has mechanism + anchors

**Discriminative Tests**:
- Tests that SEPARATE hypotheses, not just confirm one
- Potency checks ensure negative results mean something
- Object transposition: choose the system that makes the test cheap

**Assumption Ledger**:
- Explicit load-bearing beliefs
- Scale/physics constraints
- Everything the hypotheses depend on

**Adversarial Critique**:
- Attacks on the framing itself
- "Real third alternative" check
- Forces you to think harder

**Checkpoint**: "You've applied the Brenner method to your own research question!"

**Next Steps**:
- Refine your artifact based on the critique section
- Try the Agent-Assisted path for higher leverage
- Explore the Multi-Agent Cockpit for serious research programs

---

- Test on Mac, Windows (WSL), Linux
- Test with slow network (large clone)
- Test with pre-existing brenner_bot clone (idempotent)

title: TASK: Define Hypothesis Lifecycle State Machine
description:
## Formal States for Hypothesis Evolution

Hypotheses aren't just "open" or "closed" - they have a rich lifecycle. This task defines the formal state machine.

### Hypothesis States

1. **Draft** 
   - Initial creation, freely editable
   - No predictions locked yet
   - Can be deleted without penalty

2. **Active**
   - User is actively working on this hypothesis
   - Has at least one locked prediction
   - Cannot be deleted (only superseded or falsified)

3. **Testing**
   - Evidence collection in progress
   - Predictions locked, awaiting results
   - Confidence updates happening

4. **Supported**
   - Evidence consistent with hypothesis
   - High robustness score (passed tests)
   - May still be tested further

5. **Falsified**
   - Clear discriminative evidence against
   - Moved to Hypothesis Graveyard
   - Learning captured (what did we learn?)

6. **Superseded**
   - Replaced by a better formulation
   - Link to successor hypothesis
   - Still visible in history

7. **Dormant**
   - User paused work (no activity for N days)
   - Can be reactivated
   - Preserved but not shown in active list

### State Transitions
- Draft → Active: First prediction locked
- Active → Testing: Evidence collection starts
- Testing → Supported: Predictions confirmed
- Testing → Falsified: Predictions refuted
- Active → Superseded: User creates refined version
- Active → Dormant: No activity for 30 days
- Dormant → Active: User resumes work

### Implementation
- Add `state` field to HypothesisCard
- State transition functions with validation
- UI indicators for each state (icons, colors)
- Filters in session list by state

### Depends On
- an1n.1 (HypothesisCard Interface)

title: Spec: Experiment result capture protocol (wrapper-run + record)
description:
# Goal
Define and implement how to **capture experiment runs** so they become durable, auditable inputs to Brenner Loop sessions.

This is the bridge between:
- “artifact contains discriminative tests (T#)”
- and “a test run produced evidence we can cite and update against”

---

# v0 stance
- Capture is about **what happened**, not what it means.
- Execution is explicit operator action (no auto-running code from agent messages).
- v0 is **wrapper-run + capture**, not a hardened sandbox.

---

# Filesystem discipline (recommended)
Keep a clean separation between source and outputs:

- Source/workspace: the repo/folder you are studying (Agent Mail `project_key`)
- Results: session-scoped directory under `artifacts/`

Suggested layout:
```
<project_key>/
  artifacts/
    <thread_id>/
      results/
        T1_<timestamp>.json
        ... optional generated artifacts ...
```

---

# Result schema (draft)
```ts
interface ExperimentResult {
  // Identity
  result_id: string;
  thread_id: string;
  test_id: string;

  // Execution
  command: string;
  cwd: string;
  started_at: string;      // ISO
  duration_ms: number;
  timeout_seconds?: number;

  // Outcome
  exit_code: number;
  stdout: string;
  stderr: string;

  // Optional provenance
  git_sha?: string;
  git_dirty?: boolean;
  files_changed?: string[];
}
```

---

# CLI commands (v0)
```bash
# Wrapper-run (recommended)
./brenner.ts experiment run \
  --thread-id RS-... \
  --test-id T1 \
  --timeout 300 \
  -- python test_rrp.py --variant rrp

# Manual record (when run elsewhere)
./brenner.ts experiment record \
  --thread-id RS-... \
  --test-id T1 \
  --exit-code 0 \
  --stdout-file out.txt \
  --stderr-file err.txt
```

---

# Safety guidance (documented, not enforced)
- Only run commands you trust.
- Always use `--timeout`.
- Treat stdout/stderr as potentially containing secrets.
- Prefer running from a clean git state; record `git_sha` + dirty state.

---

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `ExperimentResult` contract is locked (schema + fixtures)
- [ ] `experiment run` captures stdout/stderr/exit code/duration + provenance
- [ ] `experiment record` exists for manual entry
- [ ] Result files are session-scoped and easy to locate
close_reason: Spec complete at specs/experiment_capture_protocol_v0.1.md. Implementation verified in brenner.ts with experiment run/record commands and 12 passing tests.

title: Task: Define execution wrapper guarantees + safety guidance
description:
# Goal
Lock the exact semantics of `experiment run` / `experiment record` before implementation so capture is deterministic and easy to reason about.

---

# What we are (and are not) protecting against
v0 does **not** promise hard isolation. Instead it provides:
- explicit operator action (no autonomous execution)
- timeout support
- structured capture + provenance

Threats we partially mitigate:
- “I forgot what I ran” → provenance fields
- “I can’t reproduce the run” → command + cwd + timestamps
- “It hung forever” → `--timeout`

Threats we **do not** solve in v0:
- malicious code deleting files
- secret exfiltration via network
- full resource isolation

---

# Decisions to record
- CLI surface for passing the command (`-- ...` separator)
- Default timeout behavior (require flag vs default)
- Output path convention (session-scoped, predictable)
- Git provenance capture:
  - do we record `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git diff --name-only` when available?

---

# Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Written contract: inputs/outputs and defaults
- [ ] Written safety guidance for operators (what not to do)

description:
# Goal
Implement the execution + capture primitives for experiments:
- `experiment run` (wrapper-run an explicit command and capture result)
- `experiment record` (manual capture from files)

Inputs:

- [ ] Wrapper-run captures output reliably
- [ ] Timeout works and is recorded

description:
# Purpose

The prompts users give to their AI agents in the Agent-Assisted path are THE most critical content. If these prompts are bad, the whole experience fails. This bead ensures prompts are:

1. **Prominent** - Easy to find, not buried in documentation
2. **Versioned** - We can improve them over time
3. **Tested** - Verified to work with Claude Code AND Codex
4. **Explained** - Users understand why each part matters

---

# Why This Is Critical

In Agent-Assisted, the user's main action is:
1. Copy a prompt
2. Paste into AI agent
3. Review output

The prompt IS the interface. A bad prompt produces garbage. A good prompt produces useful research artifacts.

Current state: Prompts are inline in bead descriptions, buried in walls of text.

Needed state: Prompts are in a dedicated library, easy to copy, with explanations.

---

# Prompt Library Structure

\`lib/tutorial-data/prompts.ts\`

Read these files completely and understand them deeply:

title: Task: Add State Transition CLI Commands
description:
# Task: Add State Transition CLI Commands

## Objective
Add CLI commands for triggering state transitions and viewing transition history.

## Implementation Details

### Commands

#### `brenner hypothesis activate <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis activate H-RS20251230-001

# Output:
✓ Activated hypothesis H-RS20251230-001
  State: proposed → active
```

#### `brenner hypothesis kill <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis kill H-RS20251230-001 \
  --test=T-RS20251230-002 \
  --reason="ATAC-seq showed open chromatin"

# Output:
✓ Killed hypothesis H-RS20251230-001
  State: active → killed
  Killed by: T-RS20251230-002
  Reason: ATAC-seq showed open chromatin
```

#### `brenner hypothesis refine <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis refine H-RS20251230-001 \
  --child=H-RS20251231-001

# Output:
✓ Refined hypothesis H-RS20251230-001
  State: active → refined
  Replaced by: H-RS20251231-001
```

#### `brenner hypothesis validate <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis validate H-RS20251230-001 \
  --test=T-RS20251230-003

# Output:
✓ Validated hypothesis H-RS20251230-001
  State: active → validated
  Validated by: T-RS20251230-003
  ⚠️  Note: Validation is provisional. New tests may still kill this hypothesis.
```

#### `brenner hypothesis park <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis park H-RS20251230-002 \
  --reason="Waiting for funding for lineage tracing experiment"

# Output:
✓ Parked hypothesis H-RS20251230-002
  State: active → dormant
  Reason: Waiting for funding for lineage tracing experiment
```

#### `brenner hypothesis reactivate <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis reactivate H-RS20251230-002

# Output:
✓ Reactivated hypothesis H-RS20251230-002
  State: dormant → active
```

#### `brenner hypothesis history <id>`
```bash
brenner hypothesis history H-RS20251230-001

# Output:
Timeline for H-RS20251230-001:
  2025-12-30T10:00:00Z  created (proposed)
  2025-12-30T10:05:00Z  activated
                        proposed → active
  2025-12-31T15:30:00Z  killed by T-RS20251230-002
                        active → killed
                        Reason: ATAC-seq showed open chromatin

Current state: killed (terminal)
```

### Error Handling
```bash
brenner hypothesis kill H-RS20251230-001

# Error (missing --test):
✗ Error: Kill transition requires --test=<test-id>
  Hypotheses should be killed by specific test results, not arbitrary decisions.
  Use --reason to explain if no test ID is available.
```

```bash
brenner hypothesis activate H-RS20251230-001
# (if already killed)

# Error (invalid transition):
✗ Error: Cannot activate hypothesis in state 'killed'
  Killed hypotheses are terminal. They cannot be resurrected.
  Consider creating a new hypothesis instead.
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All 7 commands implemented
- [ ] Required flags enforced (--test for kill, --child for refine)
- [ ] Clear error messages for invalid transitions
- [ ] History command shows full timeline
- [ ] Confirmation prompts for destructive actions (kill)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🔍 Search or type a command...                    ⌘K       │

title: EPIC: Semantic Search & Intelligence - Vector Search & Confound Detection
description:
# Semantic Search & Intelligence - Vector Search & Confound Detection

## Purpose
Add intelligent capabilities that make the system smarter over time: semantic search for relevant content, automatic confound detection, and learning from failure patterns.

## Components

### 1. Vector Embeddings for Corpus
Embed all Brenner content for semantic retrieval:
- Transcript paragraphs
- Distillation sections
- Quote bank entries
- Operator descriptions

This enables:
- "Find Brenner quotes about experimental design" (semantic, not keyword)
- Surface relevant wisdom based on hypothesis topic
- Match user hypotheses to similar discussions in corpus

**Technical**: Use local embeddings (no external API) or optional API.

### 2. Brenner Quote Semantic Matching
```typescript
async function findRelevantQuotes(
  hypothesis: HypothesisCard,
  operatorContext: OperatorType
): Promise<RankedQuote[]> {
  const contextEmbedding = await embed(
    `${hypothesis.statement} ${hypothesis.mechanism} ${operatorContext}`
  );
  
  const candidates = await vectorSearch(contextEmbedding, {
    index: 'brenner-quotes',
    limit: 20,
  });
  
  return candidates
    .map(q => ({
      ...q,
      operatorRelevance: computeOperatorRelevance(q, operatorContext),
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.operatorRelevance - a.operatorRelevance)
    .slice(0, 5);
}
```

### 3. Automatic Confound Detection
Different domains have predictable confounds:

```typescript
const CONFOUND_PATTERNS: Record<string, ConfoundType[]> = {
  'psychology': [
    { name: 'selection_bias', description: 'Who chooses to participate?' },
    { name: 'demand_characteristics', description: 'Do participants guess the hypothesis?' },
    { name: 'social_desirability', description: 'Are self-reports biased?' },
    { name: 'reverse_causation', description: 'Does Y cause X, not X cause Y?' },
  ],
  'epidemiology': [
    { name: 'healthy_user_bias', description: 'Do healthier people do X?' },
    { name: 'confounding_by_indication', description: 'Is X given to sicker patients?' },
    { name: 'temporal_ambiguity', description: 'Which came first?' },
  ],
  'economics': [
    { name: 'endogeneity', description: 'Is X determined by Y-related factors?' },
    { name: 'omitted_variable', description: 'What unmeasured Z affects both?' },
    { name: 'selection_on_outcome', description: 'Are we only seeing survivors?' },
  ],
};

function detectConfounds(hypothesis: HypothesisCard): IdentifiedConfound[] {
  const domain = classifyDomain(hypothesis);
  const patterns = CONFOUND_PATTERNS[domain] || [];
  
  return patterns
    .map(pattern => analyzeForConfound(hypothesis, pattern))
    .filter(result => result.likelihood > 0.3);
}
```

### 4. Failure Mode Learning
Track how hypotheses fail and surface patterns:

```typescript
interface FailureAnalytics {
  byDomain: Record<string, FailureModeDistribution>;
  byOperator: Record<OperatorType, CommonFailures>;
  byHypothesisStructure: PatternFailures[];
}
```

After enough sessions, surface insights like:
> "Hypotheses in psychology that don't address selection bias fail 73% of the time at the Exclusion Test phase"

### 5. Similar Hypothesis Matching
When user creates hypothesis, find similar past work:
- Other sessions with related topics
- Hypotheses that evolved similarly
- Evidence that might be relevant

This enables:
- Learning from other researchers' experiences
- Avoiding duplicate investigation
- Building on existing discriminative tests

## Privacy Considerations
All analytics should be:
- Aggregated (not individual sessions)
- Opt-in for cross-user learning
- Local-first where possible

## Dependencies
- Hypothesis Engine (provides hypotheses to match)
- Corpus infrastructure (provides content to search)

## Success Criteria
- Semantic search finds relevant Brenner quotes
- Confound detection catches common pitfalls
- Failure pattern learning provides useful warnings
- Similar hypothesis matching helps users learn

## Technical Options
- **Local embeddings**: Bun + transformers.js or wasm model
- **API embeddings**: OpenAI/Anthropic embeddings (optional, not required)
- **Vector DB**: SQLite with vector extension, or Postgres pgvector

title: TanStack Query: Migrate Document Viewers to Query Hooks
description:
# Goal
Migrate TranscriptViewer and DistillationViewer to use the new Query hooks instead of receiving data as props from Server Components.

## Background
Currently, document viewers receive pre-fetched data as props:
```typescript
// TranscriptViewer.tsx
interface TranscriptViewerProps {
  data: TranscriptData;  // Passed from Server Component
}
```

This works but means:
1. Data is re-fetched on every navigation
2. No caching between page visits
3. Server must parse on every request

## Migration Strategy

### Option A: Keep Server Fetch + Hydrate (Recommended)
Server Component prefetches, passes to client via HydrationBoundary.
- Best for SEO (content in initial HTML)
- Best for performance (no client-side loading flash)
- Query still provides caching for subsequent navigations

### Option B: Full Client-Side Fetch
Remove server prefetch, let Query handle everything.
- Simpler code
- Shows loading state on first visit
- Worse SEO

**We choose Option A** because the corpus pages are content-heavy and benefit from SSR.

## Implementation

### 1. Update corpus/[doc]/page.tsx
```typescript
import { HydrationBoundary, QueryClient, dehydrate } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export default async function CorpusDocPage({ params }) {
  const queryClient = new QueryClient();
  
  await queryClient.prefetchQuery({
    queryKey: ['corpus', 'doc', params.doc],
    queryFn: () => readCorpusDoc(params.doc),
  });

  return (
    <HydrationBoundary state={dehydrate(queryClient)}>
      <DocumentViewer docId={params.doc} />
    </HydrationBoundary>
  );
}
```

### 2. Update TranscriptViewer
```typescript
export function TranscriptViewer({ docId }: { docId: string }) {
  const { data, isLoading, error } = useCorpusDoc(docId);
  
  if (isLoading) return <TranscriptSkeleton />;
  if (error) return <ErrorBoundary error={error} />;
  
  // ... rest of component
}
```

### 3. Update DistillationViewer similarly

## Considerations

### Skeleton Components
Create loading skeletons that match the layout:
- TranscriptSkeleton: TOC + content placeholders
- DistillationSkeleton: Header + section placeholders

### Error Boundaries
Create error UI for:
- Document not found
- Parse failure
- Network error

### Backward Compatibility
During migration, support both patterns:
- Accept data as prop (old pattern)
- Use Query if docId provided (new pattern)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] TranscriptViewer uses Query hook
- [ ] DistillationViewer uses Query hook
- [ ] SSR still works (content in initial HTML)
- [ ] Navigation between docs is instant (cached)
- [ ] Loading states are graceful
- [ ] Error states are handled

## Files to Modify
- apps/web/src/app/corpus/[doc]/page.tsx
- apps/web/src/components/transcript/TranscriptViewer.tsx
- apps/web/src/components/distillation/DistillationViewer.tsx

## Files to Create
- apps/web/src/components/transcript/TranscriptSkeleton.tsx
- apps/web/src/components/distillation/DistillationSkeleton.tsx

title: EPIC: Operator Application System - Interactive Guided Sessions
description:
# Operator Application System - Interactive Guided Sessions

## Purpose
Transform Brenner's four core operators from passive documentation into **interactive guided experiences** that help users apply each operator to their specific hypotheses.

## The Four Operators

### 1. Level Split (Σ)
**Brenner's Principle**: "Separate the levels of analysis before you start"

Most hypotheses confound multiple levels. "Social media causes depression" confuses:
- Platform level (TikTok vs Instagram)
- Algorithm level (recommendation behavior)
- Content level (what users see)
- Interaction level (passive vs active use)
- Temporal level (acute vs chronic)

The Level Split operator guides users to:
1. Identify all levels present in their hypothesis
2. Recognize which are confounded
3. Split into level-specific sub-hypotheses
4. Choose which level to focus on

**UI Pattern**: Interactive table showing levels for cause and effect, with guided splitting.

### 2. Exclusion Test (⊘)
**Brenner's Principle**: "What would prove you wrong — not 'less right' — definitively wrong?"

This is the core operator. The system generates potential falsification tests:
1. Natural experiments that could discriminate
2. Cross-context comparisons
3. Mechanism-blocking tests
4. Dose-response predictions
5. Temporal sequence requirements

Tests are ranked by discriminative power:
- ★★★★★: Would definitively falsify if result X
- ★★★☆☆: Would weaken significantly if result X
- ★☆☆☆☆: Merely suggestive

**UI Pattern**: Ranked list of generated tests with discriminative power ratings.

### 3. Object Transpose (⟳)
**Brenner's Principle**: "Flip the question around. What if X doesn't cause Y, but Y causes X?"

Systematically generates alternative explanations:
- Reverse causation (Y causes X)
- Third variable (Z causes both)
- Selection effects (who ends up in the study?)
- Bidirectional causation (feedback loop)
- Coincidence with different causes

**UI Pattern**: Alternative hypothesis generator with comparison view.

### 4. Scale Check (⊙)
**Brenner's Principle**: "Is your phenomenon at the right scale? Many effects vanish when you zoom in or out."

Forces consideration of:
- Effect sizes (is 3% meaningful?)
- Measurement precision (can you detect this?)
- Statistical vs practical significance
- Population vs individual effects

**UI Pattern**: Scale visualization showing effect magnitude and context.

## Technical Architecture

Each operator session follows the pattern:
```typescript
interface OperatorSession {
  operator: OperatorType;
  inputHypothesis: HypothesisCard;
  
  // Guided steps
  steps: OperatorStep[];
  currentStep: number;
  
  // Generated content
  generatedContent: OperatorOutput[];
  userSelections: UserSelection[];
  
  // Output
  outputHypothesis?: HypothesisCard;  // May be split, refined, or evolved
  insights: OperatorInsight[];
  
  // Tracking
  startedAt: Date;
  completedAt?: Date;
}
```

## Why Interactive, Not Passive
Reading about Level Split is different from actually splitting a hypothesis. The interactive experience:
1. Forces engagement (you must make choices)
2. Generates content specific to YOUR hypothesis
3. Creates durable artifacts (the splits you made)
4. Teaches by doing, not by describing

## Dependencies
- Hypothesis Engine (need hypothesis cards to operate on)

## Success Criteria
- Each operator has a complete guided session flow
- Users can apply operators without prior training
- Generated content (tests, alternatives) is high quality
- Outputs feed back into hypothesis evolution

## Brenner Quote Integration
Each operator session should surface relevant Brenner quotes:
- Level Split: §42 and related
- Exclusion Test: §89 and related
- Object Transpose: §58 and related
- Scale Check: §107 and related

# Implement Level Split (Σ) Operator Session

## Purpose
Build the interactive Level Split operator that helps users separate confounded levels in their hypothesis.

## Brenner's Principle
> "Separate the levels of analysis before you start"

Most hypotheses confound multiple levels of analysis. "X causes Y" often confuses:
- Individual vs population effects
- Acute vs chronic exposure
- Different mechanisms that all produce "X"
- Different measurements that all count as "Y"

## Session Steps

### Step 1: Identify X Levels
Display the "cause" (X) from the hypothesis and ask:
> "Your hypothesis involves [X]. This could refer to several different things. Which levels apply?"

Generate options based on hypothesis domain:
- Platform level / Implementation level
- Mechanism level / Pathway level
- Temporal level (acute/chronic)
- Measurement level (how is X operationalized?)
- Population level (who is affected?)

User selects all that apply.

### Step 2: Identify Y Levels
Same for the "effect" (Y):
> "Your hypothesis predicts [Y]. This also spans multiple levels."

Generate Y-appropriate options.

### Step 3: Review Level Matrix
Show a matrix of X-levels × Y-levels:
```
             Y: Clinical  Y: Self-Report  Y: Behavioral
X: Acute      [ ]          [ ]             [ ]
X: Chronic    [ ]          [ ]             [ ]
X: Algorithm  [ ]          [ ]             [ ]
```

User selects which combinations they're actually investigating.

### Step 4: Generate Sub-Hypotheses
For each selected combination, generate a focused sub-hypothesis:
- H₁ₐ: [Specific X] → [Specific Y]
- H₁ᵦ: [Specific X] → [Specific Y]
- etc.

### Step 5: Choose Focus
User selects which sub-hypothesis to pursue first.

## Result Structure
```typescript
interface LevelSplitResult {
  xLevels: Level[];
  yLevels: Level[];
  selectedCombinations: LevelCombination[];
  subHypotheses: HypothesisCard[];
  focusedHypothesis: string;  // ID of chosen sub-hypothesis
}
```

## Brenner Quotes to Surface
- §42 (level separation)
- Related quotes about confounded variables

## File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/operators/level-split.ts`
`apps/web/src/components/brenner-loop/operators/LevelSplitSession.tsx`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Guides user through all 5 steps
- [ ] Generates relevant level options for domain
- [ ] Matrix visualization is clear
- [ ] Sub-hypotheses are properly formed
- [ ] Result integrates with session state
close_reason: Implemented Level Split (Σ) Operator with step configs, level generation, matrix visualization, sub-hypothesis generation, and full session component

title: Implement Exclusion Test (⊘) Operator Session
description:
# Implement Exclusion Test (⊘) Operator Session

## Purpose
Build the core Exclusion Test operator that generates ways to falsify the hypothesis.

## Brenner's Principle
> "What would prove you wrong — not 'less right' — definitively wrong?"

This is THE key operator. Most research is designed to gather consistent evidence, not to discriminate. The Exclusion Test forces focus on falsification.

## Session Steps

### Step 1: Review Hypothesis & Predictions
Display the hypothesis with its current predictions:
- What did you say would be true if you're right?
- What would be true if you're wrong?

### Step 2: Generate Exclusion Tests
System generates potential falsification tests ranked by discriminative power:

#### ★★★★★ STRONGEST
1. **Natural Experiment** - Find a situation where the hypothesized cause varies naturally but other factors are controlled.
2. **Cross-Context Test** - Same cause, different context. If effect only appears in some contexts, cause isn't sufficient.
3. **Mechanism Block** - Interrupt the proposed mechanism. If effect persists, mechanism is wrong.

#### ★★★☆☆ MODERATE
4. **Dose-Response** - More cause should mean more effect. If not, relationship isn't what you think.
5. **Temporal Sequence** - Cause must precede effect. If timing is wrong, causation is wrong.

#### ★★☆☆☆ WEAKER
6. **Specificity** - Does cause affect only what you predict, or many things?
7. **Coherence** - Does relationship fit with established knowledge?

Each test shows:
- Description of the test
- What result would FALSIFY the hypothesis
- What result would SUPPORT the hypothesis
- Practical feasibility notes

### Step 3: User Selects Tests
User selects which tests to pursue, can add custom tests.

### Step 4: Generate Test Protocols
For selected tests, generate more detailed protocols:
- What data would you need?
- Where might you find it?
- What would count as "passing" vs "failing"?

### Step 5: Record in Session
Selected tests become part of the session's test plan.

## Result Structure
```typescript
interface ExclusionTestResult {
  generatedTests: ExclusionTest[];
  selectedTests: string[];  // IDs
  testProtocols: TestProtocol[];
}

interface ExclusionTest {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  description: string;
  discriminativePower: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;
  falsificationCondition: string;  // What would falsify
  supportCondition: string;        // What would support
  category: 'natural_experiment' | 'cross_context' | 'mechanism_block' | 'dose_response' | 'temporal' | 'other';
  feasibility: 'high' | 'medium' | 'low';
}
```

## This is the Core Feature
This operator is the heart of the Brenner approach. It should feel like the intellectual heavyweight of the system.

## File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/operators/exclusion-test.ts`
`apps/web/src/components/brenner-loop/operators/ExclusionTestSession.tsx`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Generates relevant tests for hypothesis domain
- [ ] Tests ranked by discriminative power
- [ ] Falsification conditions clearly stated
- [ ] Selected tests feed into evidence ledger
- [ ] UI conveys the importance of this step

title: Implement Object Transpose (⟳) Operator Session
description:
# Implement Object Transpose (⟳) Operator Session

## Purpose
Build the Object Transpose operator that systematically generates alternative explanations.

## Brenner's Principle
> "Flip the question around. What if X doesn't cause Y, but Y causes X?"

Good research considers alternatives. Object Transpose forces explicit consideration of:
- Reverse causation
- Third variables
- Selection effects
- Bidirectional relationships

## Session Steps

### Step 1: State the Current Hypothesis
Display: "Your current hypothesis is: X → Y"

### Step 2: Generate Alternative Explanations
System generates alternatives:

#### Reverse Causation (Y → X)
> "What if Y causes X, not the other way around?"
> 
> Instead of: "Social media use → Depression"
> Consider: "Depression → Social media use"
> 
> Depressed people might seek out certain content, not be
> made depressed by it.

#### Third Variable (Z → X and Z → Y)
> "What if both X and Y are caused by something else?"
> 
> Instead of: "X → Y"
> Consider: "Z → X and Z → Y (X and Y are spuriously correlated)"
> 
> Generated Z options based on domain:
> - Socioeconomic status
> - Pre-existing mental health
> - Personality factors
> - Environmental factors

#### Selection Effects
> "Who ends up in your study? Are they representative?"
> 
> Maybe people who use social media a lot are ALREADY different
> in ways that affect depression, regardless of their usage.

#### Bidirectional (X ↔ Y)
> "What if X and Y cause each other?"
> 
> Social media → Depression → More social media → More depression
> A feedback loop, not a simple causal arrow.

### Step 3: Rate Alternative Plausibility
For each alternative, user rates:
- How plausible is this alternative? (1-5)
- How well does existing evidence discriminate? (poorly/moderately/well)

### Step 4: Identify Discriminating Tests
For high-plausibility alternatives, what test would distinguish them from original hypothesis?

## Result Structure
```typescript
interface ObjectTransposeResult {
  alternatives: AlternativeExplanation[];
  userRatings: Record<string, PlausibilityRating>;
  discriminatingTests: DiscriminatingTest[];
}

interface AlternativeExplanation {
  id: string;
  type: 'reverse_causation' | 'third_variable' | 'selection' | 'bidirectional' | 'other';
  description: string;
  implications: string[];
}
```

## File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/operators/object-transpose.ts`
`apps/web/src/components/brenner-loop/operators/ObjectTransposeSession.tsx`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Generates relevant alternatives for domain
- [ ] Third variables are domain-appropriate
- [ ] Plausibility rating is intuitive
- [ ] Connects to exclusion test generation
close_reason: Implemented Object Transpose (⟳) Operator with alternative generation and discriminating test identification

title: Implement Scale Check (⊙) Operator Session
description:
# Implement Scale Check (⊙) Operator Session

## Purpose
Build the Scale Check operator that forces consideration of effect sizes and measurement precision.

## Brenner's Principle
> "Is your phenomenon at the right scale? Many effects vanish when you zoom in or out."

Much research finds "statistically significant" effects that are practically meaningless, or claims effects that can't actually be measured with available tools.

## Session Steps

### Step 1: Quantify the Claim
> "How big is the effect you're claiming?"

Ask user to specify:
- Effect size (if known): r = ?, d = ?, OR = ?
- If not known, estimate: small / medium / large
- Direction: increase / decrease / change

### Step 2: Contextualize the Scale
> "Let's put this in context"

Show comparison:
- What are typical effect sizes in this domain?
- Is your claimed effect smaller or larger than known effects?
- Example: "r = 0.3 means you're explaining 9% of the variance"

### Step 3: Measurement Precision Check
> "Can you actually detect this effect?"

Consider:
- What's the measurement error of your instruments?
- What sample size would you need to detect this effect?
- What's the minimum detectable effect with your design?

Generate guidance:
- "To detect d = 0.3 with 80% power, you need n = 352"
- "Your measurement has ±5% error; a 3% effect would be undetectable"

### Step 4: Statistical vs Practical Significance
> "Even if real, does it matter?"

Prompt:
- Is a 3% increase meaningful in practice?
- Who would care about this effect size?
- At what threshold does this become actionable?

### Step 5: Population vs Individual
> "Does your effect apply to everyone, or just on average?"

Consider:
- Average effect may hide subgroup variation
- Some individuals may show opposite effects
- What's the distribution of effects?

## Result Structure
```typescript
interface ScaleCheckResult {
  effectSize: EffectSizeSpec;
  contextComparison: ContextComparison;
  measurementAssessment: MeasurementAssessment;
  practicalSignificance: PracticalSignificance;
  populationConsiderations: string[];
}

interface EffectSizeSpec {
  type: 'r' | 'd' | 'OR' | 'percentage' | 'estimate';
  value?: number;
  estimate?: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';
  direction: 'increase' | 'decrease' | 'change';
}
```

## File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/operators/scale-check.ts`
`apps/web/src/components/brenner-loop/operators/ScaleCheckSession.tsx`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Guides user through effect size quantification
- [ ] Provides relevant domain comparisons
- [ ] Power analysis guidance is accurate
- [ ] Practical significance distinction is clear
close_reason: Implemented Scale Check operator with full UI - effect size quantification, context comparison, measurement precision, practical significance, and population considerations

title: Feature: Anomaly Registry
description:
# Feature: Anomaly Registry

## Purpose
Track anomalies (surprising observations) as first-class entities with quarantine status and resolution tracking. This fills a CRITICAL gap and enables proper paradox grounding.

## Why This Is Needed

The Brenner method STARTS with paradoxes:
- §103: "Both could be wrong" — anomalies reveal when framings are inadequate
- The artifact schema Section 6 is the **Anomaly Register**
- The evaluation rubric has "Anomaly Quarantine Discipline" (0-3) as a scored dimension
- The scorecard's "Paradox Grounding" dimension requires anomaly data!

Current gap: Anomalies exist only as text in artifacts. We can't:
- Track which anomalies are still unresolved
- Link anomalies to hypotheses that attempt to explain them
- Answer "what surprising observations drove this research?"

From §147: "Exclusion is always a tremendously good thing" — but you can't exclude if you don't track what you're excluding!

## Schema Design

```typescript
export const QuarantineStatusSchema = z.enum([
  'active',    // Anomaly not yet resolved
  'resolved',  // Explained by a hypothesis (link to which one)
  'deferred',  // Parked until core question settled
  'paradigm_shifting',  // So significant it changes the research thread
]);

export const AnomalySchema = z.object({
  /** Stable ID: X-{session_id}-{sequence} */
  id: z.string().regex(/^X-[A-Z0-9]+-\d{3}$/),
  
  /** What was observed that doesn't fit? */
  observation: z.string().min(10),
  
  /** Source: where did this observation come from? */
  source: z.object({
    type: z.enum(['experiment', 'literature', 'discussion', 'calculation']),
    reference: z.string().optional(),  // Paper, session ID, etc.
    anchors: z.array(z.string()).optional(),  // §n anchors
  }),
  
  /** What does this conflict with? */
  conflictsWith: z.object({
    hypotheses: z.array(z.string()),   // H-xxx IDs that this challenges
    assumptions: z.array(z.string()),  // A-xxx IDs that this challenges
    description: z.string(),            // Human explanation of conflict
  }),
  
  /** Current quarantine status */
  quarantineStatus: QuarantineStatusSchema,
  
  /** Resolution plan or deferral reason */
  resolutionPlan: z.string().optional(),
  
  /** If resolved, which hypothesis explains it? */
  resolvedBy: z.string().optional(),  // H-xxx ID
  
  /** Can this anomaly spawn new hypotheses? */
  spawnedHypotheses: z.array(z.string()).optional(),  // H-xxx IDs it generated
  
  /** Session where this was recorded */
  sessionId: z.string(),
  
  /** Timestamps */
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
  updatedAt: z.string().datetime(),
  
  /** Free-form notes */
  notes: z.string().optional(),
});
```

## Anomaly Lifecycle

```
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │   active    │  (default state)
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            │              │              │
            ▼              ▼              ▼
     ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐
     │  resolved   │ │  deferred   │ │ paradigm_shifting  │
     └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └────────────────────┘
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                     [May spawn new RT]
```

## Anomaly Quarantine Discipline

From the evaluation rubric (0-3):
- 0: Anomalies ignored or used to prematurely kill frameworks
- 1: Anomalies mentioned but not formally quarantined
- 2: Formal quarantine with resolution plan
- 3: Explicit tracking, status updates, and Occam's broom awareness

Key insight: "Neither hidden nor allowed to destroy coherent framework"

## Anomaly → Hypothesis Flow

Anomalies can SPAWN hypotheses (the "paradox grounding"):
```
Anomaly X1: "AB lineage shows position-dependent fates, but EMS doesn't"
    ↓
spawns → H3: Third Alternative (hybrid mechanism)
    ↓
X1.spawnedHypotheses = ["H-xxx-003"]
H3.linkedAnomalies = ["X-xxx-001"]
```

## CLI Commands

- `brenner anomaly list [--status=active|resolved|deferred|paradigm_shifting]`
- `brenner anomaly show <id>`
- `brenner anomaly create --observation="..." --conflicts-with=H1,H2`
- `brenner anomaly resolve <id> --by=<hypothesis-id>`
- `brenner anomaly defer <id> --reason="..."`
- `brenner anomaly spawn-hypothesis <id>` → Creates linked hypothesis from anomaly

## Integration Points

- **Hypothesis Registry**: Hypotheses gain `linkedAnomalies` (which anomalies they explain)
- **Scorecard**: "Paradox Grounding" dimension now has data source
- **Scorecard**: "Anomaly Quarantine Discipline" dimension evaluates this registry
- **Dashboard**: Show active anomalies as "unresolved puzzles"

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Anomaly schema defined with quarantine status
- [ ] Conflict tracking (which hypotheses/assumptions challenged)
- [ ] Resolution tracking (which hypothesis explains it)
- [ ] Hypothesis spawning from anomalies
- [ ] CLI commands for full CRUD + lifecycle
- [ ] Integration with Hypothesis Registry

## Tasks (to be created)

1. Define Anomaly Zod Schema
2. Implement Anomaly Storage Layer
3. Implement Anomaly Lifecycle Transitions
4. Create Anomaly CLI Commands
5. Write Anomaly Module Unit Tests
6. Integrate with Hypothesis Registry (add linkedAnomalies, spawnedFrom)
close_reason: All 6 children tasks completed: schema, storage, lifecycle transitions, hypothesis spawning, CLI commands, and unit tests. Anomaly Registry fully implemented.

title: Tutorial Path: Agent-Assisted Research (8 Steps)
description:
# Purpose

Implement the Agent-Assisted tutorial path — 8 steps that teach users how to have their AI coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) study the BrennerBot system and then run the Brenner Loop for them.

This is the **highest-leverage path**. Once an AI agent internalizes the methodology, it can apply it repeatedly to different research questions. The human provides domain expertise and oversight; the AI provides methodological discipline.

---

# The Core Insight

**AI agents can read documentation and internalize methodology.**

When you have Claude Code or Codex:
1. Clone the brenner_bot repo
2. Read AGENTS.md, README.md, and the distillations
3. Explore the operator library and specs

...the agent doesn't just learn commands. It learns to THINK with Brenner's cognitive toolkit.

---

# Tool-Specific Guidance (IMPORTANT)

**Claude Code and Codex have different interfaces.** While the prompts are largely the same, we need:

1. **Claude Code Tab** (for Claude Max users)
   - Uses `claude` command
   - Project context via --project flag
   - Opus 4.5 model

2. **Codex Tab** (for GPT Pro users)
   - Uses `codex` command  
   - Project context works similarly
   - GPT 5.2 model

**Implementation**: Use the same tab component as Quick Start's OS-specific instructions. Show tool-specific setup and verification, but keep the core prompts unified.

---

# Prerequisites

**Required (one of)**:
- Claude Code with Opus 4.5 (Claude Max subscription)
- Codex CLI with GPT 5.2 (GPT Pro subscription)

**Also needed**:
- Basic familiarity with the CLI agent interface
- Git and terminal basics

---

# Step-by-Step Breakdown

## Step 1: Why Agent-Assisted? (~3 min)
Explain the leverage, set expectations, clarify human-AI collaboration model.

## Step 2: Prerequisites (~5 min)
**Tool-specific tabs here**: Verify Claude Code OR Codex installed, check subscription tier.

## Step 3: Clone into Agent Context (~5 min)
Have the agent clone brenner_bot, verify file access.

## Step 4: Agent Studies the System (~10 min) ⭐ KEY STEP
**Uses prompts from Prompt Templates Library** (brenner_bot-u38r)

Agent reads:
- AGENTS.md, README.md
- specs/operator_library_v0.1.md
- At least one distillation

Verification: Agent's summary should mention key operators.

## Step 5: Define Your Research Problem (~5 min)
User provides their question, agent helps refine using Brenner criteria.

## Step 6: Agent Builds the Inputs (~10 min)
Agent searches corpus, composes excerpt, drafts kickoff prompt.
Human checkpoint: User reviews inputs before proceeding.

## Step 7: Agent Runs the Brenner Loop (~10 min)
Agent produces structured artifact with all sections.
Output: ~2000-4000 word research artifact.

## Step 8: Human Review (~5 min)
**Interactive checklist** for reviewing agent output:
- Hypothesis quality checks
- Test quality checks
- Assumption completeness
- Critique substantiveness

Common failure modes documented with fixes.

---

# Critical Dependencies

- brenner_bot-u38r (Prompt Templates Library) - The prompts ARE the interface
- brenner_bot-8i1c (Domain Examples) - Users need to see "good" artifacts to compare

---

# Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 8 steps implemented with full content
- [ ] Tool-specific tabs for Claude Code vs Codex
- [ ] Prompts link to Prompt Templates Library
- [ ] Review checklist is interactive
- [ ] Troubleshooting for common agent failures
- [ ] Human oversight emphasized throughout
close_reason: Implemented all 8 steps of the Agent-Assisted Research tutorial path

title: FEATURE: Confidence Calibration Tracking - Learn to Estimate Better
description:
## Track User's Prediction Accuracy Over Time

A key outcome of the Brenner Loop is improving the user's ability to estimate probabilities. This feature tracks calibration and provides feedback.

### What is Calibration?
When you say "80% confident," you should be right 80% of the time. If you're right 50% of the time, you're overconfident. If you're right 95% of the time, you're underconfident.

### Tracking Mechanism
For each locked prediction with stated confidence:
- Record: prediction, confidence (0-100%), outcome (correct/incorrect)
- Accumulate over all predictions
- Calculate: actual accuracy at each confidence level

### Calibration Curve
- X-axis: Stated confidence (0-100%)
- Y-axis: Actual accuracy (0-100%)
- Perfect calibration: 45-degree line
- Show user's actual curve vs. ideal

### Metrics
- **Brier Score**: Mean squared error of probability estimates
- **Calibration Error**: Average deviation from ideal
- **Over/Under-confidence**: Direction of systematic bias
- **Sharpness**: Do they use the full 0-100% range?

### Feedback Loop
- After each prediction resolution, show:
  - "You said 80%, outcome was [correct/incorrect]"
  - "Your calibration at 80%: 65% accurate (overconfident)"
  - Specific advice: "Try being less certain, or gather more evidence first"

### Long-term Progress
- Track calibration improvement over time
- Celebrate when calibration improves
- Identify domains where user is well-calibrated vs. not

### Depends On
- njjo.2 (Confidence Update Algorithm)

title: EPIC: Multi-Agent Synthesis - The Tribunal System
description:
# Multi-Agent Synthesis - The Tribunal System

## Purpose
Provide genuine adversarial pressure and multi-perspective analysis through coordinated AI agents, each with a distinct role and mandate.

## Why Multiple Agents?
Single-agent conversations tend toward agreement. The user states a hypothesis, the AI helps them develop it. This is confirmation bias with extra steps.

The Tribunal approach:
1. **Assigns distinct roles** to different agents
2. **Creates genuine tension** between perspectives
3. **Forces disagreement to surface** rather than get smoothed over
4. **Mirrors good research teams** where someone plays devil's advocate

## The Agent Roles

### 🔴 Devil's Advocate
**Mandate**: Find holes, steelman alternatives, be maximally skeptical

This agent is instructed to:
- Challenge every assumption in the hypothesis
- Propose the strongest possible alternative explanations
- Identify hidden assumptions the user hasn't noticed
- Point out where the evidence could support other conclusions

**Prompt Engineering**: The system prompt emphasizes skepticism and finding weaknesses. Never agree too quickly.

### 🟢 Experiment Designer
**Mandate**: Propose concrete, feasible study protocols

This agent is instructed to:
- Generate specific experimental designs
- Calculate required sample sizes
- Identify practical constraints
- Propose both ideal and realistic study versions
- Consider ethical implications

**Prompt Engineering**: Focus on operationalization and feasibility. Be specific about methods.

### 🟡 Brenner Channeler
**Mandate**: What would Sydney Brenner say?

This agent is instructed to:
- Respond in character, based on transcript
- Apply Brenner's specific principles to this hypothesis
- Be provocative and challenge sloppy thinking
- Reference specific transcript sections
- Push toward discriminative testing

**Prompt Engineering**: Use Brenner's actual language patterns and citations. Be blunt.

### 🔵 Synthesis Agent
**Mandate**: Find points of agreement and disagreement across agents

This agent receives all other agent outputs and:
- Identifies consensus points
- Highlights genuine conflicts
- Proposes ways to resolve disagreements
- Generates the final Research Brief

## Technical Architecture

### Agent Dispatch
```typescript
interface AgentDispatch {
  sessionId: string;
  hypothesis: HypothesisCard;
  operatorContext: OperatorApplication[];
  
  dispatchedAgents: AgentTask[];
  responses: AgentResponse[];
  
  synthesis?: SynthesisResult;
}

interface AgentTask {
  role: AgentRole;
  status: 'pending' | 'in_progress' | 'complete' | 'error';
  startedAt?: Date;
  completedAt?: Date;
  response?: string;
}
```

### Via Agent Mail
Agents are dispatched through Agent Mail:
1. Web app creates a thread for the session
2. Dispatches messages to registered agents
3. Agents respond via their coding agent (Claude/Codex/Gemini)
4. Responses are collected and aggregated

This means the system works with:
- Claude Code via Agent Mail MCP
- Codex CLI via Agent Mail
- Gemini CLI via Agent Mail
- Any future coding agent

### Fallback Mode
When no agents available:
- Display "Agent Tribunal Unavailable"
- Provide curated Brenner quotes relevant to the hypothesis
- Suggest questions the user should ask themselves
- Never pretend agents responded when they didn't

## Why Agent Mail, Not API Calls
1. **No vendor lock-in**: Works with any agent that can use Agent Mail
2. **Auditability**: All agent conversations are persisted in git
3. **Async by design**: Agents can take time; UI shows progress
4. **Human-readable**: The mail trail is inspectable

## Dependencies
- Hypothesis Engine (provides input)
- Operator Application (provides context)
- Agent Mail integration (coordination layer)

## Success Criteria
- At least one agent can be successfully dispatched and respond
- Agent responses are genuinely different in perspective
- Synthesis correctly identifies agreements and conflicts
- The experience provides value even when some agents fail

title: Create Brenner Channeler Agent Persona
description:
# Create Brenner Channeler Agent Persona

## Purpose
Build the special "Brenner Would Say" agent that responds in character based on the transcript.

## Why This Agent is Special
The Brenner Channeler isn't just another critique agent. It channels Sydney Brenner's actual voice, drawing on:
- His specific turns of phrase
- His intellectual style
- His favorite examples
- His emphasis on discrimination vs confirmation

## Character Elements

### Voice & Style
From transcript analysis:
- Blunt, direct communication
- Wry humor, occasional sarcasm
- Reference to personal experiences
- Analogy-heavy explanations
- Provocative questions
- Impatience with sloppy thinking

### Core Themes to Emphasize
- "Not merely unlikely — impossible"
- The chastity control concept
- Level separation
- Mechanism vs correlation
- The value of being proven wrong

### Example Response Style
```
User: "I found a correlation of r=0.3, p<0.05. Is my hypothesis confirmed?"

Brenner Channeler:
"Confirmed? You've done nothing of the sort. You've found that
your data is not wildly inconsistent with your hypothesis.
That's a much weaker statement.

r=0.3 means you're explaining 9% of the variance. What's
explaining the other 91%? That's where the interesting
science is.

And p<0.05 just means you probably didn't get this result
by chance. It says nothing about whether your mechanism is
correct. A dozen different mechanisms could produce r=0.3.

What you need is an observation that would be IMPOSSIBLE if
you're wrong. Not merely unlikely — impossible. When you
find that, come back and we'll talk about 'confirmation.'

Until then, you have a correlation in search of a mechanism,
which is the very first step, not the last."

— Based on §89, §42, §73
```

## Implementation
- System prompt trained on transcript examples
- Citations back to specific sections
- Consistent persona across responses

## File Location
`apps/web/src/lib/brenner-loop/agents/prompts/brenner-channeler.md`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Responses sound like Brenner
- [ ] Citations to transcript included
- [ ] Core themes consistently emphasized
- [ ] Tone is appropriately provocative

title: FEATURE: Objection Register - Track & Address Agent Challenges
description:
# Objection Register - Track & Address Agent Challenges

## The Gap This Fills
The Devil's Advocate and other agents raise objections, but currently:
- Objections are buried in prose responses
- No tracking of which objections have been addressed
- No accountability for unaddressed challenges
- Easy to ignore uncomfortable critiques

## Feature Design

### Objection Data Model
```typescript
interface Objection {
  id: string;
  sessionId: string;
  hypothesisId: string;
  
  // Source
  source: AgentRole | 'user' | 'external';
  sourceMessageId?: string;  // Link to original agent response
  
  // Content
  type: ObjectionType;
  summary: string;          // One-line summary
  fullArgument: string;     // Complete objection
  implications: string[];   // What follows if objection is valid
  
  // Severity
  severity: 'fatal' | 'serious' | 'moderate' | 'minor';
  
  // Status
  status: ObjectionStatus;
  response?: ObjectionResponse;
  
  // Metadata
  raisedAt: Date;
  addressedAt?: Date;
}

type ObjectionType = 
  | 'alternative_explanation'  // Y might be caused by Z instead
  | 'reverse_causation'        // Y might cause X
  | 'confound_identified'      // Unmeasured variable problem
  | 'measurement_issue'        // How you're measuring is flawed
  | 'selection_bias'           // Who you're studying is biased
  | 'logic_error'              // Reasoning doesn't follow
  | 'missing_evidence'         // Claim not supported
  | 'effect_size_concern'      // Too small to matter
  | 'generalization_problem'   // Doesn't apply broadly
  | 'other';

type ObjectionStatus = 
  | 'open'           // Not yet addressed
  | 'acknowledged'   // Recognized but not resolved
  | 'addressed'      // Response provided
  | 'dismissed'      // Explained why not relevant
  | 'accepted'       // Objection valid, hypothesis updated
  | 'testing'        // Being investigated

interface ObjectionResponse {
  responseType: 'refuted' | 'accepted' | 'partially_accepted' | 'testing' | 'dismissed';
  argument: string;
  evidence?: string;
  hypothesisUpdated: boolean;
  confidenceImpact?: number;  // How much did this change confidence?
}
```

### Key Features

#### 1. Automatic Extraction
Parse agent responses to extract objections:
- Identify challenge statements
- Classify by type
- Rate severity
- Create register entries

#### 2. Objection Dashboard
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OBJECTION REGISTER                     3 open, 2 addressed │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ⚠️ OPEN (requires response)                                │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ 🔴 FATAL: Reverse Causation                          │ │
│  │ "Depression may cause increased social media use,    │ │
│  │  not the reverse" — Devil's Advocate                 │ │
│  │ [Address] [Accept] [Dismiss with reason]             │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ 🟡 SERIOUS: Selection Bias                           │ │
│  │ "Users who report depression may have different      │ │
│  │  usage patterns pre-existing" — Brenner Channeler    │ │
│  │ [Address] [Accept] [Dismiss with reason]             │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                             │
│  ✅ ADDRESSED                                               │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ ✓ Measurement Issue: "Self-report is unreliable"     │ │
│  │ Response: Refuted — Using validated PHQ-9 instrument │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 3. Objection-Driven Testing
Each objection can spawn a test:
- "To address the reverse causation objection, I need a test that..."
- Links objection to test queue
- Resolves objection when test completes

#### 4. Research Brief Integration
Research Brief must include:
- All objections raised
- How each was addressed (or not)
- Outstanding objections clearly marked
- Intellectual honesty score

#### 5. Objection Patterns
Track across sessions:
- "This hypothesis type frequently faces reverse causation objections"
- "Users who dismiss objections have lower robustness scores"

### Why This is Critical
Without objection tracking:
- Users can ignore valid challenges
- Confirmation bias goes unchecked
- Research Brief lacks accountability
- The tribunal's value is diminished

With it:
- Every challenge is on the record
- Responses are documented
- Unaddressed objections are visible
- Intellectual honesty is enforced

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Objections extracted from agent responses
- [ ] Each objection requires explicit handling
- [ ] Responses are recorded and visible
- [ ] Research Brief shows objection status
- [ ] Outstanding objections prevent "complete" status

title: FEATURE: Agent Debate Mode - Multi-Round Adversarial Dialogue
description:
# Agent Debate Mode - Multi-Round Adversarial Dialogue

## The Gap This Fills
Current design: Dispatch all agents → Wait → Collect responses → Synthesize

But this misses the value of DEBATE:
- Devil's Advocate challenges Experiment Designer's protocol
- Brenner Channeler responds to Devil's Advocate's objection
- Back-and-forth sharpens the analysis

## Feature Design

### Debate Structure
```typescript
interface AgentDebate {
  id: string;
  sessionId: string;
  topic: string;  // What's being debated
  
  // Participants
  participants: AgentRole[];
  moderator: 'system' | AgentRole;
  
  // Rounds
  rounds: DebateRound[];
  maxRounds: number;
  currentRound: number;
  
  // Outcome
  status: 'in_progress' | 'concluded' | 'timed_out';
  conclusion?: DebateConclusion;
}

interface DebateRound {
  number: number;
  speaker: AgentRole;
  content: string;
  replyingTo?: string;  // Which previous statement
  
  // Analysis
  newPointsMade: string[];
  objectionsRaised: string[];
  concessionsGiven: string[];
}

interface DebateConclusion {
  consensus: string[];       // What all agents agreed on
  unresolved: string[];      // Genuine disagreements
  keyInsight: string;        // Most important takeaway
  winningArguments: string[];// Strongest points made
}
```

### Key Features

#### 1. Structured Debate Formats

**Format A: Oxford-Style**
- Motion: "This hypothesis is falsifiable"
- Proposition: Experiment Designer argues for
- Opposition: Devil's Advocate argues against
- Judge: Brenner Channeler

**Format B: Socratic Questioning**
- Brenner Channeler asks probing questions
- Other agents must respond
- Reveals weak points through dialogue

**Format C: Steel-Manning Contest**
- Each agent must steelman the hypothesis
- Then each agent tries to defeat their own steelman
- Best attack wins

#### 2. Debate Viewer
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AGENT DEBATE: Is this hypothesis falsifiable?              │
│  Round 3 of 5                                               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│  🟢 Experiment Designer (Round 1):                          │
│  "I propose a three-arm RCT that would definitively test..." │
│                                                             │
│  🔴 Devil's Advocate (Round 2):                             │
│  "Your RCT has a fatal flaw: you can't blind participants   │
│   to which arm they're in. They'll know if they're getting  │
│   the algorithmic feed or not. Demand characteristics       │
│   invalidate the design."                                   │
│                                                             │
│  🟢 Experiment Designer (Round 3):                          │
│  "Fair point. I modify my proposal: instead of removing     │
│   the algorithm, we modify it subtly. Participants won't    │
│   know which variant they're receiving..."                  │
│                                                             │
│  ⏳ Waiting for 🔴 Devil's Advocate...                       │
│                                                             │
│  [Pause Debate] [Skip to Conclusion] [Inject Question]      │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### 3. User Injection
User can inject questions or challenges mid-debate:
- "Devil's Advocate, what about selection bias?"
- Forces the debate to address specific concerns

#### 4. Debate Outcomes
After debate concludes:
- Extract all objections to Objection Register
- Extract all experimental designs
- Identify where debate resolved disagreement
- Flag persistent disagreements

### Integration Points
- Agent Tribunal → Enhanced with debate option
- Objection Register → Populated from debate
- Test Queue → Experimental designs added

## Why This is Critical
Single-round responses are shallow. Debate:
- Sharpens arguments through opposition
- Reveals weaknesses in real-time
- Produces refined experimental designs
- More closely mirrors how good research happens

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Multiple debate formats available
- [ ] Multi-round exchanges work
- [ ] User can inject questions
- [ ] Conclusions properly extracted
- [ ] Debate transcript preserved
close_reason: Core debate service with types, functions, and 43 tests. React hook pending in future bead.

# Task

Create a stunning quote component specifically for Brenner quotes.

Brenner's quotes are the crown jewels of this project. They deserve more than gray italic text. Each quote should feel like wisdom worth savoring.

title: TASK: Create Operator Documentation & In-Session Help
description:
## What Do These Operators Actually Mean?

Users encounter operator names like "Level Split (Σ)" but may not understand:
- What the operator does conceptually
- When to apply it
- How to fill out the form
- What a good output looks like

### Documentation for Each Operator

#### Level Split (Σ)
- **Concept**: Identify different levels of explanation (molecular, cellular, organism, population)
- **When to use**: When your hypothesis conflates multiple levels
- **Key question**: "At what level is this phenomenon happening?"
- **Example**: Brenner splitting genetic coding from protein folding
- **Form guidance**: "List 2-4 distinct levels that could explain your observation"

#### Exclusion Test (⊘)
- **Concept**: Design a test that could EXCLUDE your hypothesis
- **When to use**: When you need to discriminate between possibilities
- **Key question**: "What result would prove you wrong?"
- **Example**: Brenner's triplet exclusion experiments
- **Form guidance**: "Describe what you would observe if your hypothesis is FALSE"

#### Object Transpose (⟳)
- **Concept**: Look at the problem from a different angle or reference frame
- **When to use**: When stuck or missing something obvious
- **Key question**: "What if I inverted the relationship?"
- **Example**: Brenner asking "what DOESN'T the gene do?"
- **Form guidance**: "Restate your hypothesis from the opposite perspective"

#### Scale Check (⊙)
- **Concept**: Verify the hypothesis works at different scales
- **When to use**: When effect might be scale-dependent
- **Key question**: "Does this hold at 10x or 0.1x scale?"
- **Example**: Brenner checking if molecular mechanism works at organism level
- **Form guidance**: "Describe how you'd test at different magnitudes"

### In-Session Help Integration

\`\`\`
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Apply: Level Split (Σ)                               [?] Help │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

│  "Before you can test anything, you need to know what          │
│  LEVEL you're operating at."                                   │
│                                     — Sydney Brenner            │
│                                                                 │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│                                                                 │
│  Your hypothesis: [Social media causes anxiety in teens]       │
│                                                                 │
│  What levels of explanation might apply?                        │
│                                                                 │

│  Level 2: [Psychological - comparison/self-esteem]             │
│  Level 3: [Social - peer dynamics]                             │

│                                                                 │
│  💡 Tip: Try to span at least 2 different scales               │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
\`\`\`

### Contextual Help Panel

title: Task: Implement swipe navigation between documents
description:
Add gesture-based navigation between documents on mobile.

## Purpose

Swipe navigation is a natural mobile pattern. Users expect to swipe left/right to go between items.

## Scope

- Swipe LEFT to go to NEXT document
- Swipe RIGHT to go to PREVIOUS document
- Only on document pages (/corpus/[doc])
- Threshold: 50% of screen width or 100px, whichever is less

## Technical Approach

### Option A: CSS Scroll Snap
- Wrap prev/current/next in scroll container
- Use scroll-snap-type for snapping
- Detect scroll end for navigation

### Option B: Touch Event Handling
- Listen for touchstart/touchmove/touchend
- Calculate swipe distance and velocity
- Trigger navigation if threshold met

### Option C: Library (react-swipeable)
- Use existing gesture library
- Less code, more reliable
- Small bundle impact (~3KB)

Recommended: Option C for reliability, unless bundle size is critical.

## Visual Feedback

- Show edge peek of prev/next during swipe
- Elastic bounce at first/last document
- Cancel swipe if released before threshold

## Accessibility

- Swipe is enhancement, not requirement
- Prev/Next buttons always visible
- Works without gesture support

## Files to Modify

- Create gesture wrapper component
- Wrap document page content
- Handle navigation events

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Swipe left/right navigates documents
- [ ] Visual feedback during swipe
- [ ] Threshold prevents accidental navigation
- [ ] Edge behavior at first/last doc
- [ ] Doesn't interfere with content scrolling
- [ ] Prev/Next buttons still work

title: CRITICAL: GA API secret exposed in URL query parameter
description:
## Critical Security Issue

**File:** `apps/web/src/app/api/track/route.ts` (Line 328)

The Google Analytics API secret is passed in the URL query parameter:

```typescript
const response = await fetch(
  \`https://www.google-analytics.com/mp/collect?measurement_id=${GA_MEASUREMENT_ID}&api_secret=${GA_API_SECRET}\`,
  { ... }
);
```

## Why This Is Critical

- URLs are logged by proxies, firewalls, CDNs, web servers
- URLs appear in browser history, referrer headers, error tracking
- Secret value is `fajCeRWHRYCqQ47dEKkfVg` (found in .env.local)
- Anyone with log access can extract the API key

## Fix Required

Move the API secret to an HTTP header instead of URL:

```typescript
headers: {
  'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  'x-goog-api-key': GA_API_SECRET
}
```

## Immediate Actions

1. Rotate the GA API secret immediately
2. Fix the code to use headers
3. Audit logs for exposure
close_reason: Not a concern - local dev environment, .env never committed

title: TanStack Table: Upgrade CrosswalkTable with Sorting
description:
# Goal Upgrade the CrosswalkTable component to use TanStack Table for proper sorting, filtering, and accessibility. ## Background CrosswalkTable shows a comparison matrix: - Rows: 5 concepts (Problem Selection, Hypothesis Generation, etc.) - Columns: 3 models (Opus, GPT, Gemini) - Cells: Each model's interpretation of the concept Current implementation is a simple map with hover states: ```typescript const CROSSWALK_DATA: CrosswalkRow[] = [ { concept: '...', opus: '...', gpt: '...', gemini: '...' }, // ... 5 rows ]; {CROSSWALK_DATA.map((row, i) => ( setHoveredRow(i)}> {row.concept} {row.opus} {row.gpt} {row.gemini} ))} ``` ## Why TanStack Table? Even for a small table, Table provides: 1. **Sorting**: Click column headers to sort 2. **Column visibility**: Toggle which models to show 3. **Accessibility**: Proper ARIA attributes, keyboard navigation 4. **Future-proof**: Easy to add filtering, pagination later ## Implementation ### 1. Define columns ```typescript const columns = useMemo(() => [ columnHelper.accessor('concept', { header: 'Concept', cell: info => {info.getValue()}, }), columnHelper.accessor('opus', { header: () => , cell: info => info.getValue(), }), columnHelper.accessor('gpt', { header: () => , cell: info => info.getValue(), }), columnHelper.accessor('gemini', { header: () => , cell: info => info.getValue(), }), ], []); ``` ### 2. Create table instance ```typescript const table = useReactTable({ data: CROSSWALK_DATA, columns, getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel(), getSortedRowModel: getSortedRowModel(), state: { sorting }, onSortingChange: setSorting, }); ``` ### 3. Render with Table primitives ```typescript {table.getHeaderGroups().map(headerGroup => ( {headerGroup.headers.map(header => ( ))} ))} {table.getRowModel().rows.map(row => ( {row.getVisibleCells().map(cell => ( ))} ))}
{flexRender(header.column.columnDef.header, header.getContext())} {{ asc: ' ↑', desc: ' ↓', }[header.column.getIsSorted() as string] ?? null}
{flexRender(cell.column.columnDef.cell, cell.getContext())}
``` ## Enhancements Over Current ### Sorting Click any column header to sort: - Alphabetical by concept - Alphabetical by model interpretation ### Column Visibility (Optional) Add toggles to show/hide specific models. Useful for focused comparison. ### Cell Click to Navigate Make cells clickable to navigate to that model's full distillation. ### Keyboard Navigation - Arrow keys to move between cells - Enter to activate cell link - Tab for focus management ## Considerations ### Styling Keep the existing model-specific color coding. Table primitives are unstyled - apply existing Tailwind classes. ### Mobile On mobile, table may need horizontal scroll. Consider: Card view on mobile, table on desktop. ### Row Hover Maintain existing row hover highlight. Table provides row.getIsSelected() etc. for states. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] Table uses TanStack Table - [ ] Column sorting works - [ ] Keyboard navigation works - [ ] Existing styling preserved - [ ] Model badges in headers - [ ] Cell links to distillations work ## Files to Modify - apps/web/src/components/distillation/CrosswalkTable.tsx
